meta.title: The TSMC Style Course
meta.subtitle: One model. One café. 419 ways to make a picture — all images generated by Muse.
meta.model: TSMC — 'The Quiet Queenmaker' of Silicon Wars — drawn from her character sheet in every picture.

lessons.title: Made of What? Drawing and Painting Media
lessons.bigIdea: Before style comes stuff. Every picture is made of a material, and the material leaves fingerprints.
lessons.intro: Our model sits in the same café pose for every picture in this lesson. Only the medium changes: pencil, ink, chalk, water, oil, pixels. Watch how each material pushes the same scene toward a different mood — soft, sharp, glowing, flat. Learning to name the medium is the first skill of looking at art.
lessons.exercise: Pick two pictures of the same pose and list three things that changed besides color. Edges? Texture? How dark the darkest dark is?

styles.name: Graphite Drawing
styles.blurb: The humblest medium: a pencil. Everything is built from gray — light grays for silk and skin, deep grays for shadow — with no color to hide behind.
look: Shading is blended smoothly, like breath on glass
Edges are soft where light wraps around the figure
The whole scene fits in one family of grays

styles.name: Pen and Ink
styles.blurb: A pen cannot erase and cannot do gray directly — grays are faked with hatching, thousands of tiny parallel lines. The result is crisp, decisive and a little nervous.
look: Look for cross-hatched shadows on the skirt and chair
Lines get denser where things get darker
Highlights are just paper left empty

styles.name: Ink Wash
styles.blurb: Ink thinned with water into a ladder of grays, laid down in flowing washes. One brushstroke must do the work of a whole shadow — there is no going back.
look: Big soft pools of gray form the background
A few dry-brush strokes snap the details into focus
The mood is quiet, like the moment before rain

styles.name: Charcoal Drawing
styles.blurb: Burnt willow ground into sticks: charcoal gives the blackest blacks and the smudgiest edges of any drawing medium. Artists smear it with fingers and lift it with erasers.
look: Deep velvety darks behind the figure
Edges dissolve where the artist smudged
Bright highlights were erased back into the paper

styles.name: Colored Pencil
styles.blurb: Color built from dozens of transparent layers of pencil. Slower than paint, more controlled than pastel — every hair and thread can be placed exactly.
look: Fine grain from the paper shows through the color
Colors are mixed by layering, not on a palette
Edges stay sharp and deliberate everywhere

styles.name: Soft Pastel
styles.blurb: Pastel sticks are almost pure pigment, so colors glow with a powdery, light-scattering softness. It is drawing and painting at the same time.
look: A velvety bloom softens every surface
Colors sit on top of each other like dust
Skin and cloth share the same chalky light

styles.name: Watercolor
styles.blurb: Water does half the work. Pigment pools, blooms and dries lighter than it looks wet, and the white of the paper becomes the light in the picture.
look: Transparent washes let the paper shine through
Edges bloom where wet paint met wet paper
Nothing is fully opaque — even shadows glow

styles.name: Gouache
styles.blurb: Watercolor's matte, opaque cousin — designers loved it because it photographs flat and covers mistakes. Colors dry chalky, even and poster-like.
look: Flat, even color areas with little shine
Light colors sit cleanly on top of dark ones
The finish looks like a printed illustration

styles.name: Acrylic Painting
styles.blurb: Invented in the 20th century, acrylic dries in minutes and can imitate oil, watercolor or plastic-smooth flatness. The café scene gets crisp edges and a modern, satin finish.
look: Clean edges mixed with smoothly blended passages
Colors stay bright and slightly synthetic
No canvas glow — the surface is calm and matte-satin

styles.name: Oil Painting
styles.blurb: The prestige medium of European art for 500 years: slow-drying, blendable, and capable of glowing translucent layers called glazes. Skin and silk were its specialties.
look: Soft, seamless blending on the face and hands
Deep colors glow as if lit from inside
Brushwork disappears into polished finish

styles.name: Egg Tempera
styles.blurb: The panel painter's medium before oil: fast, matte and precise, built from thousands of tiny hatched strokes. It gives the scene a pale, luminous, early-Renaissance stillness.
look: Fine hatched strokes model every form
Colors are pale, dry and luminous
A faint gold warmth hangs over the scene

styles.name: Buon Fresco
styles.blurb: True fresco is painted into wet lime plaster, so the image becomes part of the wall itself — which is why Giotto's work survives 700 years later. Our version even has the cracks.
look: Matte, mineral colors with no shine at all
Hairline cracks cross the surface
It reads as a wall, not a page — flat and architectural

styles.name: Digital Painting
styles.blurb: Painting with software: infinite undo, perfect gradients, brushes that imitate everything in this lesson. The challenge flips — with no material resistance, the artist must invent their own limits.
look: Airbrush-smooth gradients with painterly accents
Lighting is polished and cinematic
No paper grain, no cracks — a surface that never existed physically

styles.name: Vector Illustration
styles.blurb: Not pixels but equations: every shape is a clean curve that can scale forever without blurring. The café becomes a diagram of itself — all signal, no texture.
look: Perfectly smooth edges at any size
Flat color shapes with a few clean gradients
Details are simplified into symbols

styles.name: Manga Ink and Screentone
styles.blurb: Black ink plus screentone — printed dot patterns that fake gray. Manga artists turn economy into style: a few tones, bold blacks, and speed of reading above all.
look: Dot-pattern tones shade the skirt and background
Solid blacks anchor hair, chair and shadows
The drawing stays light and quick to read

styles.name: Anime Cel Shading
styles.blurb: Classic TV animation painted characters on clear cels: flat color, one shadow tone, bold outlines. Zero blending — every form is a decision about where light stops.
look: Exactly two tones per surface: lit and shadow
Thick, confident outlines
The background is softer than the character, so she pops forward

styles.name: Silverpoint
styles.blurb: Before pencils existed, artists drew with a silver wire on specially coated paper. The line starts faint and slowly darkens as the silver tarnishes, and it can never be erased — every stroke is a commitment.
look: Fine warm-grey lines on a pale, prepared ground
Precise hatching builds all the shading
The drawing feels delicate and ghostly, with no dark blacks anywhere

styles.name: Red Chalk and Conté
styles.blurb: Sanguine is a stick of rust-red earth that Leonardo and Michelangelo used for life studies. Its warm color flatters skin, and it blends softly with a fingertip, so the café scene feels like a page from an Old Master sketchbook.
look: Everything is drawn in one warm red-brown color
Shading is softly blended, like a study of flesh
The cream paper shows through as the lightest light

styles.name: Oil Pastel
styles.blurb: Oil pastels are pigment mixed with oil and wax into a fat, buttery crayon. They lay down thick, vivid color that never fully dries, so the café scene looks rich, waxy and a little bit smeary.
look: Thick, buttery strokes you can almost feel
Bright colors layered on top of each other
The edges of each stick mark stay visible in the surface

styles.name: Encaustic
styles.tag: Hot wax painting, ancient to modern
styles.blurb: Encaustic means painting with molten beeswax mixed with pigment — a technique so durable that 2,000-year-old Egyptian portraits still glow. The wax gives our scene a luminous, slightly melted softness.
look: A waxy sheen sits over the whole surface
Edges look softly melted, as if warmed
Colors glow with the richness of an ancient Fayum portrait

styles.name: Impasto and Palette Knife
styles.blurb: Impasto is paint applied so thickly that it stands up off the canvas in ridges and peaks, often spread with a palette knife instead of a brush. Van Gogh made it famous; here it turns the café scene into a low relief sculpture of paint.
look: Paint ridges and peaks catch real-looking light
Knife marks slice flat planes through the forms
The surface has as much energy as the scene itself

styles.name: Grisaille
styles.blurb: Grisaille is painting entirely in grays, traditionally as the underlayer that later got glazed with color — or to imitate stone sculpture. With the color switched off, the café scene becomes pure light, shadow and form.
look: Every value is gray, from near-white to near-black
Forms are shaded so roundly they look carved in stone
It reads like the ghost of a painting waiting for its color

styles.name: Airbrush
styles.blurb: An airbrush sprays paint with compressed air, so there are no brushstrokes at all — just seamless, misty gradients. It was the signature tool of 1980s illustration, and it gives our scene a soft, glossy, almost photographic sheen.
look: Gradients melt into each other with no visible strokes
Highlights have a soft, sprayed halo
The finish looks polished, like a retro advertisement

styles.name: Spray Paint
styles.blurb: The spray can is the tool of street art: fast, bold, and always threatening to drift. Stencils give it sharp edges, freehand passes give it soft fades — and the café scene picks up a concrete-wall energy.
look: Overspray halos fuzz the edges of shapes
Stencil-sharp edges sit right next to soft fades
A gritty wall texture shows through the paint

styles.name: Mixed Media
styles.blurb: Mixed media means exactly what it says: paint, ink, collage, fabric scraps — whatever the picture needs, all in one work. Instead of one consistent surface, the café scene becomes a layered patchwork of clashing textures.
look: Different materials meet at visible seams
Collage and fabric pieces interrupt the painted areas
Textures clash on purpose — smooth against rough, printed against drawn

styles.name: Scratchboard
styles.blurb: A scratchboard starts completely black: a board coated in ink over white clay. The artist scratches lines through the ink to reveal the white beneath, so the picture is drawn with light instead of darkness.
look: White lines are scratched out of a black field
Fine hatching looks like an old engraving
The contrast is extreme — glowing figure, pitch-black ground

styles.name: Marker Rendering
styles.blurb: Before computers, product and car designers presented ideas in alcohol markers — fast, streaky, slightly transparent strokes that layer into rich color. Our scene gets that design-studio look, like a concept sketch pinned up for review.
look: Streaky strokes overlap where the marker passed twice
Colors bleed very slightly past their edges
The whole image feels like a polished presentation sketch

styles.name: Ballpoint Pen
styles.blurb: The humblest drawing tool of all — the pen in your pocket. Artists who master it build astonishingly rich tones from nothing but blue ink and patience, one hatched line at a time.
look: The entire picture is drawn in blue pen ink
Dense cross-hatching builds the dark tones
The ink has a slight glossy sheen, like a notebook page under light

styles.name: Casein and Distemper
styles.blurb: Casein is paint bound with milk protein, used for centuries on walls, furniture and posters. It dries fast to a chalky, completely matte finish — the café scene looks flat, powdery and quietly old-fashioned.
look: Color areas are flat and totally matte
The surface looks chalky and powdery
Light colors sit opaquely on top of dark ones, poster-style

styles.name: Fresco Secco
styles.blurb: Fresco secco means painting onto plaster that has already dried (its cousin, buon fresco, goes into wet plaster). The colors stay matte and mineral, and over centuries the wall itself starts to show through — cracks, stains and all.
look: Matte, mineral colors sit on the surface like dust
Cracks and aged plaster texture show through the paint
The image feels like a wall painting in an old church

styles.name: 3D CGI Rendering
styles.blurb: This picture was never painted or photographed — it was calculated. In a 3D render, software simulates how light bounces around a virtual scene, even how it glows through skin, until the café looks as polished as a product advertisement.
look: Light behaves perfectly — soft bounces, true reflections
Skin has a subtle translucent glow, as if lit from inside
Every surface is flawlessly clean, with no brushstroke or grain

styles.name: Matte Painting
styles.blurb: Classic movies faked their vast locations with matte paintings — enormous artworks on glass that the camera combined with a small real set. Here she sits in a real café foreground while the world behind her opens into a huge painted fab-city that was never built.
look: The foreground café feels solid and close
The background city stretches far beyond what a set could hold
The painted distance is slightly softer than the foreground, like an old film backdrop

lessons.title: Copies: Printmaking and Reproduction
lessons.bigIdea: A print is a picture made by transfer — carve it, ink it, press it, and you can make it again.
lessons.intro: Printmaking turned images into multiples centuries before photography. Each technique here — carving wood, cutting lino, etching copper, exposing a cyanotype — forces the artist to think in reversed images, layers and limited marks. Notice how the café scene survives being squeezed through each process.
lessons.exercise: Find the picture where white lines do the drawing instead of black ones. Why does carving flip the usual logic of drawing?

styles.name: Woodblock Print
styles.blurb: The image is carved into wood in reverse; what is not carved prints black. Bold shapes and knife marks are not flaws — they are the medium thinking out loud.
look: Thick black shapes carry the composition
White lines are carved, not drawn
The texture of the wood grain peeks through

styles.name: Ukiyo-e
styles.blurb: Japan's 'pictures of the floating world': separate carved blocks for each color, printed in perfect registration. Flat color, elegant line, and design sense that later stunned Paris.
look: Flat color areas bounded by a key-block line
Patterned textiles and screens fill the background
Four variants show different print moods — dark mica, pattern, actor-print boldness

styles.name: Linocut
styles.blurb: Linoleum is softer than wood, so lines swing in bold curves. The 20th-century favorite for posters and protest art: cheap, fast, unmistakable.
look: Sweeping carved curves instead of fine detail
High black-and-white contrast
One accent color — wine red — does the storytelling

styles.name: Copperplate Etching
styles.blurb: The artist draws through wax on copper; acid bites the lines; ink hides in the grooves. Rembrandt's medium — capable of spiderweb delicacy and deep, warm darks.
look: Everything is built from fine line networks
Tones are warm and antique, like old book plates
The longer you look, the more lines you find

styles.name: Lithography
styles.blurb: A greasy crayon draws on limestone; water and ink do the rest. Uniquely among print methods, it preserves the exact feel of a crayon or brush stroke.
look: Soft, grainy crayon texture in the shading
Tones feel drawn, not carved or etched
The mood is of a 19th-century Paris poster

styles.name: Screenprinting
styles.blurb: Each color is pushed through its own stenciled screen, so images arrive in flat, separable layers — the technique of Warhol and of every band T-shirt since.
look: Color arrives in flat, even layers
Slight misregistration charm at the edges
It looks printed, bold and reproducible

styles.name: Cyanotype
styles.blurb: Iron salts and sunlight: expose, rinse, and everything turns Prussian blue. Anna Atkins used it for the first photographically illustrated book in 1843.
look: Only blue and white exist in this world
Edges are soft, like shadows of real objects
The café feels like a blueprint of a memory

styles.name: Generative and Plotter Art
styles.blurb: A computer writes the rules; a pen plotter draws them — thousands of precise lines whose density becomes shading. The artist's hand moves from drawing to designing the system that draws.
look: Shading is made only of line density
Lines are perfectly regular, faintly mechanical
A single wine-red ink breaks the monochrome

styles.name: Engraving
styles.blurb: An engraver cuts lines directly into a copper plate with a sharp tool called a burin, inks the grooves, and presses paper into them. Masters like Dürer made lines that swell and taper with musical control — and our café is rebuilt entirely from those disciplined black lines.
look: Lines swell in the middle and taper to points
Shading is made of fine parallel and crossed lines
Crisp black ink sits on warm cream paper

styles.name: Drypoint
styles.blurb: In drypoint, the needle scratches the plate and throws up a ragged metal lip called the burr, which catches extra ink. That accident is the point: the lines print fuzzy and velvety, with the sketchy energy Rembrandt loved.
look: Lines have soft, fuzzy edges instead of crisp ones
Darks are rich and velvety, almost smoky
The drawing feels spontaneous, like a sketch that happened to be printed

styles.name: Aquatint
styles.blurb: Most prints draw with lines; aquatint draws with tones. A dusting of resin on the plate lets acid bite thousands of tiny pits, printing as grainy washes of gray — the technique behind Goya's darkest, moodiest images.
look: Shadows are grainy washes of gray, not lines
The mood is brooding and atmospheric, pure Goya
Thin etched lines only accent the tonal masses

styles.name: Mezzotint
styles.blurb: Mezzotint works backwards: the artist roughens the whole plate so it would print solid black, then burnishes areas smooth so they hold less ink. Light is literally polished out of darkness, giving the café a candlelit, velvet softness.
look: The image emerges from deep black toward the light
Gradients are velvety with almost no hard lines
Highlights glow softly, like candlelight on skin

styles.name: Wood Engraving
styles.blurb: Wood engraving cuts into the dense end grain of a block with burins, so the printable lines are the white cuts themselves. It powered the great illustrated books of the 1800s — think of Gustave Doré's dramatic scenes — with incredible fine detail.
look: Fine white lines are cut into black areas
Detail is dense and jewel-like, book-illustration style
Dramatic light bursts out of deep shadow

styles.name: Monotype
styles.blurb: A monotype is a painting made on a smooth plate and pressed onto paper exactly once — so, unlike other prints, there is only ever one. Degas adored the soft, ghostly images it produced; our café has that same one-chance, painterly blur.
look: Edges are soft and slightly ghostly
Ink textures look painted rather than drawn
The image feels spontaneous — a painting that was printed, once

styles.name: Chiaroscuro Woodcut
styles.blurb: Renaissance printmakers wanted woodcuts with real shading, so they carved several blocks — one for the lines, others for flat tones of brown and ochre. Layered together, the café scene gains the light-and-shadow drama Italians called chiaroscuro.
look: Flat tones of brown and ochre are layered like steps
A separate line block draws the details on top
Highlights are the bare paper left unprinted

styles.name: Pochoir Stencil
styles.blurb: Pochoir is stencil printing raised to luxury: in 1920s Paris, workshops dabbed gouache through dozens of hand-cut stencils to color fashion plates. The result is crisp, flat, jewel-bright color with a chic, decorative elegance.
look: Each color is a crisp, flat stencil shape
Colors are rich and opaque, like gouache
The scene has the elegance of a Paris fashion plate

styles.name: Letterpress
styles.blurb: Letterpress presses raised type and images into paper so hard you can feel the dent. For centuries it printed nearly every book and poster; here the café scene is bitten into soft cotton paper with that unmistakable deep impression.
look: The printed image is visibly pressed into the paper
Paper is thick, soft and cottony at the edges
Ink coverage is slightly uneven, with a handcrafted feel

styles.name: Halftone and CMYK Offset
styles.blurb: Every magazine photo is secretly made of dots. Offset printing lays down tiny halftone dots in four inks — cyan, magenta, yellow and black — and your eye mixes them into full color; zoom in on our café and the illusion falls apart into rosettes.
look: Close up, the image dissolves into rows of tiny dots
Colors are built from overlapping CMYK rosette patterns
From a distance it reads like an ordinary magazine reproduction

styles.name: Risograph
styles.blurb: The Risograph is a stencil duplicator beloved by zine makers: cheap, fast, and cheerfully imperfect. Each color is printed separately in soy-based ink, so layers drift slightly out of register — our café buzzes with fluorescent, grainy, DIY energy.
look: Color layers are slightly misregistered, offset like a double image
Inks look fluorescent and a little grainy
The texture is pure photocopied-zine energy

styles.name: Shin-hanga
styles.blurb: Shin-hanga, the 'new prints' of early 20th-century Japan, kept traditional woodblock carving and printing but borrowed Western light, shadow and atmosphere. Artists like Kawase Hasui made quiet, luminous scenes — and our café settles into that same calm.
look: A soft gradient sky fades from dark to light
Traditional carved lines carry realistic light and shadow
The mood is still and atmospheric, like evening rain

styles.name: Chinese New Year Prints
styles.blurb: For Chinese New Year, folk workshops like Yangliuqing printed cheerful woodblock images — door gods, plump babies, symbols of luck — and finished them with hand-painted color. Here she becomes an auspicious door-goddess herself, wafer in hand, in festive red and gold.
look: Bold black outlines are filled with hand-colored paint
Festive reds and golds dominate the palette
She stands front and center like a protective door-goddess

styles.name: Posada Broadside Prints
styles.blurb: José Guadalupe Posada etched zinc plates for Mexico's penny broadsheets — cheap newspapers illustrated with bold, funny, often skeleton-filled images for everyday readers. Our café is redrawn in his punchy black-line style, made to be read at a glance in a crowded street.
look: Thick, bold black lines carry the whole image
Flat, high-contrast shading with no soft tones
It looks like an illustration torn from a penny newspaper

lessons.title: Fooling the Eye: Photography and Illusion
lessons.bigIdea: A picture can pretend to be a window. Photography made that pretence cheap — and artists started asking what 'real' even means.
lessons.intro: Pictorialists made photographs look like paintings; documentary photographers chased unposed truth; photorealists painted photographs by hand; trompe-l'œil painters tried to make you reach for painted objects. This lesson now runs from photography's first silver plates to doubles and stagings — same café, many different claims about reality.
lessons.exercise: Cover the labels and sort the pictures from 'most like a dream' to 'most like evidence'. What visual clues did you use?

styles.name: Pictorialist Photography
styles.blurb: Early art photographers fought for photography's status by making it dreamy: soft focus, hand-worked prints, painterly haze. Proof, they argued, that a camera could make art.
look: Focus melts at the edges of the frame
Sepia-platinum tones, like an old photograph
Mood matters more than information

styles.name: Documentary Photography
styles.blurb: The opposite claim: the camera tells the truth. Grain, available light, an unposed instant — the café as evidence of a real afternoon.
look: Grain and imperfect light feel honest
Nothing seems arranged for your benefit
Black and white strips the scene to fact

styles.name: Photorealism
styles.blurb: Painters in the 1970s copied photographs so exactly that the painting disappears into the photo — including the photo's blur, glare and accidents. It asks: if it looks identical, what is the difference?
look: Every reflection and texture is accounted for
Even the camera's depth-of-field blur is painted
You keep forgetting it is not a photograph

styles.name: Trompe-l'œil
styles.blurb: Painting that tries to escape its own frame: painted flies, peeling corners, objects that beg to be touched. The four variants stage different tricks — a letter board, a marble ledge, a pinned note.
look: Painted shadows make objects seem to lift off the surface
One detail (a fly, a peeling corner) sells the illusion
The frame itself becomes part of the joke

styles.name: Daguerreotype
styles.blurb: The first practical photograph: a one-of-a-kind image on a silver-coated copper plate, announced in 1839. Because the plate is a mirror, the portrait seems to float in metal — tilt it and she appears and vanishes. Long exposures forced sitters into stiff formality, which gives these portraits their grave, uncanny stillness.
look: A mirror-like sheen makes the portrait shimmer like metal
Razor-fine detail sits inside a soft vignetted oval
The stiff, formal pose of an 1840s sitting

styles.name: Wet Plate and Tintype
styles.blurb: In the 1850s and 60s, photographers coated a glass plate with sticky collodion, exposed and developed it while still wet — a portable darkroom went everywhere, even to Civil War battlefields. The process is moody and imperfect: plates streak, chemicals stain, and the blacks go very deep. Our café portrait borrows that gravity.
look: Streaked plate edges and chemical stains frame the image
Blacks are deep and heavy, like old ink
A solemn, Civil War-era stillness hangs over the pose

styles.name: Straight Photography
styles.blurb: In the early 20th century, photographers like Ansel Adams rejected soft, painterly effects and demanded the camera do what only a camera can: render everything tack-sharp, with a full scale of tones from black to white. Adams called it the Zone System — planning every shade of gray in advance. Nothing here is manipulated; the clarity itself is the style.
look: Every detail is tack-sharp, front to back
A complete ladder of tones runs from deep black to clean white
No blur, no trickery — just exact, unmanipulated seeing

styles.name: Street Photography
styles.blurb: Street photographers prowl public places with small cameras, waiting for what Henri Cartier-Bresson called the decisive moment — the split second when people and geometry click into a composition. The pictures are candid: nobody poses, life blurs past, and one glance carries the scene. Here she looks up mid-crossing while strangers stream around her.
look: A candid, unposed instant — she glances up mid-crossing
Strangers blur past while she stays the still point
Black-and-white geometry locks the chaos into shapes

styles.name: Photogram
styles.blurb: A photogram is a photograph made with no camera at all: objects are laid directly on light-sensitive paper and exposed, leaving white silhouettes where they blocked the light. Man Ray called his versions rayographs and used them to make the everyday strange. Her profile, the cup and a wafer become ghosts of themselves — shadows recorded as light.
look: White silhouettes glow against pitch-black paper
Only outlines survive — profile, cup and wafer as pure shapes
No camera, no lens: the objects touched the paper themselves

styles.name: Hyperrealism
styles.blurb: Hyperrealist painters start from photographs and then out-paint them, sharpening every pore, thread and reflection until the image feels more real than reality — and slightly unreal because of it. The café scene becomes almost uncomfortable to look at: nothing is allowed to stay vague. It is photography's clarity pushed until it turns uncanny.
look: Detail is pushed past what a camera would catch
Every reflection and surface gleams with exaggerated precision
The sharpness feels slightly uncanny, like a dream in focus

styles.name: Illusionistic Ceiling Painting
styles.blurb: Baroque churches hired painters to dissolve their ceilings: painted architecture (quadratura) continues the real building upward, then opens into sky crowded with flying saints. Everything is calculated for a viewer standing far below — the Italian phrase di sotto in sù means 'from below, upward.' Here she reclines among the clouds, seen from underneath, as the painted heaven tumbles around her.
look: Painted architecture breaks open into open sky
Figures are radically foreshortened, seen from below
She reclines among clouds and tumbling bodies

styles.name: Anamorphosis
styles.blurb: An anamorphic picture is deliberately wrecked: stretched and smeared so it looks like nonsense head-on, then snaps into sense when seen from a sharp side angle or in a curved mirror. Holbein hid a smeared skull in The Ambassadors that resolves only as you walk past. Our café scene is dragged diagonally across the picture — coherence is something you have to move to earn.
look: The whole scene is stretched and smeared diagonally
Forms only make sense at a raking, side-on angle
A hidden order lurks inside apparent distortion

styles.name: Color Photography
styles.blurb: For decades, serious photography meant black and white; color was for snapshots. William Eggleston changed that in the 1970s by photographing utterly ordinary things — a tricycle, a ceiling light — in dye-transfer prints with saturated, glowing color. His lesson: the banal becomes gorgeous if you look at it completely. This unremarkable café moment gets the same luminous treatment.
look: Saturated dye-transfer color makes the ordinary glow
The subject is deliberately mundane — a snapshot moment
Color itself, not drama, is the picture's event

styles.name: Staged Photography
styles.blurb: Staged photographers build their pictures like film sets instead of finding them. Cindy Sherman starred in her own fake movie stills; Jeff Wall constructs scenes as carefully as paintings. Everything is deliberate, and the artifice is part of the point — you are meant to sense the stage machinery. Here she plays a character at the café table under cinematic light.
look: Cinematic lighting makes the café feel like a film set
She performs a role rather than simply posing
The construction is visible — the scene knows it is staged

styles.name: Düsseldorf School Photography
styles.blurb: Students of Bernd and Hilla Becher at the Düsseldorf academy made deadpan into a doctrine: photograph the same kind of thing frontally, in flat light, with zero emotion, and let order itself become the subject. Andreas Gursky scaled the approach up to enormous, hyper-detailed prints of stock exchanges and supermarkets. This portrait keeps the same cool, typological clarity.
look: A frontal, deadpan composition with no drama
Large-format precision renders every detail evenly
Emotionless clarity — order is the subject

styles.name: Fashion Photography
styles.blurb: Fashion photography sells a fantasy as much as a garment: dramatic light, sculptural poses and magazine-cover confidence turn clothing into desire. The great editorial photographers borrow from cinema and painting to make a model into an icon. Here her cleanroom tunic is styled as couture — the fab uniform, shot like a Vogue cover.
look: Dramatic studio light sculpts the pose
The cleanroom tunic is styled and worn as couture
Pure magazine-cover confidence and polish

styles.name: Double Exposure
styles.blurb: A double exposure layers two photographs in one frame, so two moments haunt each other. Film photographers made them by accident and then on purpose; portraitists love the way a face can fill with a landscape or a city. Here her portrait is ghosted together with fab machinery and city lights — the engineer and her world occupying the same skin of light.
look: Two images share one frame, each ghosting through the other
Fab machinery and city lights fill her portrait's silhouette
Edges soften where the two exposures melt together

lessons.title: The Decorated Surface: Craft, Pattern and Material
lessons.bigIdea: Not every picture hangs in a frame. Some are built from stone, glass, cloth and clay — and pattern is their language.
lessons.intro: Mosaics, stained glass, batik cloth, quilts, carved stone and glazed porcelain: these arts decorate useful or sacred surfaces, and their materials dictate their geometry. Edges become lead lines, grout lines, seams and glazes. Compare how each craft breaks the café scene into pieces — and why.
lessons.exercise: Choose one craft picture and imagine touching it. Where is it rough, smooth, heavy, fragile? How did the material decide the shapes?

styles.name: Byzantine-Inspired Mosaic
styles.blurb: Thousands of small cubes — tesserae — set into mortar, often against gold. Byzantine mosaics flatten figures on purpose: these are icons, not windows, meant to glow by candlelight.
look: You can see the individual cubes up close
Gold or deep color fills the background, not air
Four variants run from jewel-fine to rustic and aged

styles.name: Stained Glass
styles.blurb: A picture made of light itself: pieces of colored glass held by lead strips, designed to be read from inside a dark building with the sun behind it.
look: Black lead lines are the drawing
Colors glow instead of reflecting
Variants range from Gothic jewel tones to a minimal modern window

styles.name: Paper Collage
styles.blurb: Scissors as a drawing tool. Matisse, too ill to paint late in life, called it 'drawing with scissors' — shapes are cut first and arranged until they sing.
look: Every shape has a cut edge, not a drawn one
Flat papers overlap like leaves
The composition feels playful and movable

styles.name: Batik
styles.blurb: Hot wax is drawn onto cloth to resist dye; crack the wax and the dye bleeds into fine veins. Repeat for every color. The café becomes cloth — pattern is not decoration here, it is structure.
look: Fine crackle lines vein the colored areas
Indigo, wine and brown dominate the dye palette
Motifs repeat the way cloth patterns do

styles.name: Narrative Story Quilts
styles.blurb: Cloth pieces stitched into scenes — a tradition carried to brilliance by African American quilters like Harriet Powers and Faith Ringgold. Seams are the outlines; patterned fabrics do the shading.
look: Visible stitches outline every shape
Different cloth patterns stand in for light and shade
The surface feels warm, soft and handmade

styles.name: Carved Relief
styles.blurb: The scene is not drawn but excavated: figures rise a few centimeters from a stone panel, and raking light does the modeling. All color is gone — only depth remains.
look: One gray material makes the whole world
Shadows in the carving create the shading
Chisel texture survives in the background

styles.name: Ceramic Vessel and Glazing
styles.blurb: The picture wraps around a vase, bending with its belly. Glaze painting must predict the kiln: colors go in dull and come out glossy and transformed.
look: The scene curves around the vessel's body
Cobalt blue and enamel colors shine under glaze
The vase itself is part of the artwork, not a frame

styles.name: Tapestry
styles.blurb: Medieval tapestries were woven pictures: wool threads on a loom built up castles, hunts and gardens, and hung in drafty halls as insulation you could read. Because weaving works in blocks, forms flatten and outlines step like pixels. Behind the figures, millefleurs — thousands of tiny flowers — fill every gap. The café scene arrives woven, warm and slightly stepped.
look: The scene is built from visible warp-and-weft texture
A millefleurs field of tiny flowers fills the background
Forms flatten into woven blocks with stepped outlines

styles.name: Embroidery
styles.blurb: The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry at all but an embroidery — wool thread couched (stitched down) onto linen, telling the story of the Norman Conquest like a 70-metre comic strip. Its figures are flat, outlined and full of energy, with animals cavorting in the borders above and below. A blank band waits for the caption the embroiderers never added here.
look: Couched wool outlines give figures a stitched, drawn quality
Flat, lively figures march in narrative procession
Animals prowl the border, with a blank caption band

styles.name: Persian Carpet
styles.blurb: A Persian carpet is a garden you can walk on: thousands of hand-tied knots form a central medallion, corner spandrels and layered borders of flowers and vines. The designs descend from paradise gardens, where pattern stands in for planted beds and streams. Here the whole café scene is knotted into the carpet, and she sits inside the medallion at its heart.
look: Her figure sits inside the carpet's central medallion
Layered garden borders frame the scene in flowers and vines
A soft knotted-pile texture covers every inch

styles.name: Islamic Tilework
styles.blurb: From Iznik in Turkey to the zellige fountains of Morocco, Islamic tilework covers walls with glazed geometry: cobalt and turquoise stars, arabesques and interlocking polygons cut and fitted by hand. Because the tiles are glazed ceramic, light skims and cracks across them in a fine crackle. Her portrait is assembled from those shining pieces.
look: Cobalt and turquoise glazed tiles build the portrait
Geometric star patterns border the scene
A cracked-glaze shine catches light across the surface

styles.name: Lacquerware
styles.blurb: Lacquerware is built from dozens of coats of urushi — tree sap polished to a deep, liquid gloss, most famously in black and gold. In the maki-e technique, gold powder is sprinkled into wet lacquer to draw pictures that glow against the darkness, with mother-of-pearl inlay for sparkle. Her figure emerges in gold dust from a black panel, like a design surfacing in polished night.
look: Her figure is drawn in gold powder on deep black gloss
The surface shines like still, dark water
Mother-of-pearl inlay adds tiny points of sparkle

styles.name: Cloisonné Enamel
styles.blurb: Cloisonné means 'partitioned': thin metal wires are bent into outlines on a metal base, the cells between them filled with colored enamel paste, then the whole piece is fired until the enamel melts into glass. The result is jewel-bright, glossy and precise — color held in a golden cage. Her plaque portrait keeps every hue inside its wire walls.
look: Gold wire outlines partition every shape
Cells are filled with jewel-bright enamel color
The fired surface is glossy and glassy throughout

styles.name: Papercutting
styles.blurb: Papercutting turns a single sheet into lace: with scissors or a knife, an artist cuts away everything that is not the picture, and what survives is one connected silhouette. Chinese papercuts in red paper decorate windows at New Year; German and Polish traditions made whole farmyards from one sheet. Our scene is all red silhouette and white gaps — nothing is drawn, only removed.
look: The entire scene is one sheet of red paper
Intricate scissor-cut lace edges fringe every form
White gaps do the drawing — the picture is what was cut away

styles.name: Freestanding Sculpture
styles.blurb: A freestanding sculpture is carved or cast to be walked around — no wall behind it, no frame around it, just a figure holding its own space on a plinth. Material changes everything: marble turns flesh luminous, bronze goes dark and permanent, wood keeps the warmth of the tree, terracotta stays humble and earthy. Here she stands four times in a row, once in each material, like a museum experiment.
look: Four statues of her stand side by side on museum plinths
White marble, dark bronze, warm wood and terracotta compare directly
Each material changes the mood of the identical pose

styles.name: Pietra Dura and Marquetry
styles.blurb: Pietra dura — 'hard stone' — is painting with rock: marble, jasper, lapis and other stones are cut into shapes and fitted together so precisely that the seams nearly vanish, then polished to a shine. Florentine workshops made tabletops and portraits this way; marquetry does the same in wood veneer. Her portrait is assembled from polished stone pieces, each color a different rock.
look: The portrait is assembled from cut pieces of colored stone
Polished seams join marble and semi-precious inlay
Every color is a real material, not paint

styles.name: Blown Glass
styles.blurb: Glassblowers on the Venetian island of Murano gather molten glass on a pipe, blow it into bubbles and shape it in seconds before it cools — a craft of speed, breath and firelight. The finished glass stays translucent, so light passes through the figure instead of bouncing off it. She becomes a small glass figurine, café props and all, glowing faintly from the furnace.
look: She is a figurine of translucent colored glass
Tiny glass café props share the same see-through glow
Furnace-orange reflections warm the cool glass

styles.name: Beadwork
styles.blurb: Beadwork builds pictures one glass seed bead at a time — thousands of them, stitched or loomed into a surface that works exactly like pixels. Cultures from West Africa to Native North America turned beads into portraits, regalia and coded patterns. Zoom in on this portrait and she dissolves into beads; step back and she reassembles.
look: Thousands of tiny glass beads form the portrait
Each bead works like a single pixel
The beaded tapestry texture shimmers at the surface

styles.name: Basketry
styles.blurb: Basketry is weaving in three dimensions: grasses, reeds or bark are coiled and stitched in spirals until a vessel — or here, a flat panel — holds its shape. The spiral is the signature: each round of stitching climbs on the last, leaving a visible whirl of fiber. Her figure is woven from dyed grasses, dry and warm to the eye.
look: Spiral coil stitches wind visibly across the panel
Her figure is woven from dyed grasses
A dry, fibrous texture replaces every painted surface

styles.name: Featherwork
styles.blurb: In Aztec Mexico, featherworkers called amanteca made mosaics of iridescent feathers — hummingbird green, quetzal gold-green, scarlet — glued feather by feather into images that shift color as you move. Feather panels were treasured more than gold. Her image shimmers in layered green and gold plumage, changing with the light like a living surface.
look: Her image is built from iridescent green and gold feathers
The layered surface shimmers and shifts with the light
Feather tips form a soft, scaled texture everywhere

styles.name: Goldwork
styles.blurb: Goldwork is embroidery with metal: gold threads too stiff to pass through cloth are laid on the surface and couched — stitched down with silk — sometimes over padding for raised relief. It dressed altars, court robes and military uniforms in ceremonial shine. On crimson silk, her figure is worked in couched gold, glowing like a vestment.
look: Couched gold threads draw the figure on crimson silk
Padded areas rise in low relief
A ceremonial, altar-cloth shine covers the work

styles.name: Ivory Carving
styles.blurb: Japanese okimono are small decorative carvings, often in ivory, made to display on a shelf — netsuke's larger cousins, carved with jeweler's precision. The material is creamy, fine-grained and warm, and rewards tiny detail: a whole world at miniature scale. Here she sits at a tiny café table as an ivory figurine, every accessory carved to scale.
look: A miniature figurine of her sits at a tiny café table
Creamy ivory grain gives the surface a warm smoothness
Netsuke-level precision in every small accessory

styles.name: Paper Marbling
styles.blurb: Marbling — ebru in Turkish — paints on water: pigments are floated on a thickened bath, combed into peacock-feather patterns, then captured by laying paper on the surface. No two sheets can ever match. In this version her silhouette rises out of the swirling combed color, half portrait and half tide pool.
look: Her silhouette emerges from swirling, combed pigment
Peacock-feather patterns ripple across the surface
The design was floated on water before it touched paper

styles.name: Azulejo
styles.blurb: Azulejos are the painted tin-glazed tiles that skin Portuguese churches, stations and palaces — most famously in blue and white, a palette borrowed from Chinese porcelain. Each tile is painted by hand, so a big scene is a grid of small paintings with grout lines running through it. The café scene spreads across the tiles, broken and rejoined by the grid.
look: Blue-and-white painted tiles carry the whole café scene
A grouted grid breaks the image into hand-painted squares
The porcelain palette keeps everything cobalt and white

lessons.title: World Traditions I: The Ancient and Medieval World
lessons.bigIdea: Realistic perspective is one culture's choice, not a law. The oldest picture-makers solved 'how to show a person' in strikingly different ways.
lessons.intro: Start on a cave wall and walk forward 30,000 years: Egyptian-style registers, Greek marble, Roman mosaics, Persian reliefs, gold-ground icons from Byzantium to Russia, and Islamic pages where pattern and calligraphy carry the image. As you compare, ask what each culture valued enough to draw carefully — and what it happily flattened or ignored.
lessons.exercise: Find a picture where space is shown by stacking things upward instead of shrinking them with distance. Which tradition is it, and what does that choice make clearer?

styles.name: Ancient Egyptian Wall Painting
styles.blurb: Egyptian figures combine the most recognizable view of each body part: head in profile, eye frontal, shoulders frontal, legs in profile. Not a mistake — a 3,000-year information system.
look: Profile head with a frontal eye
Flat mineral colors inside firm outlines
Hieroglyph-like signs and register lines organize the wall

styles.name: Greek Vase Painting
styles.blurb: Athenian painters told myths on wine vessels: first as black silhouettes with scratched details, later reversed — red figures reserved against a black ground, allowing painted interior lines.
look: Figures wrap around the curve of an amphora
Black silhouettes carry incised detail
The red of the clay is one of the 'colors'

styles.name: Medieval Manuscript Illumination
styles.blurb: Monks and court artists lit up books with gold: miniature paintings inside decorated letters and margins crawling with vines, beasts and jokes. The page, not the wall, was Europe's picture gallery for centuries.
look: Real gold areas catch the light first
Borders teem with plants and tiny creatures
Decorative script lines complete the page

styles.name: Persian Manuscript Painting
styles.blurb: Illustrations for the Shahnameh and court poetry: jewel colors, gold skies, architecture cut open like a dollhouse, and gardens in eternal spring. Space stacks upward in tiers instead of receding.
look: A gold or midnight sky ignores natural light
Figures are small, refined and numerous
Pattern covers every surface — tile, textile, garden

styles.name: Paleolithic Cave Painting
styles.blurb: The oldest pictures we know: Stone Age artists drew animals on cave walls using ground-up earth pigments — red and yellow ochre, black charcoal — blown or smeared onto the rock. There is no ground line and no perspective, just the wall itself and the flickering shapes on it.
look: Her figure is drawn like a simple painted sign among hand stencils and bison
Earth colors only — ochre reds, yellows and charcoal black
The rough rock surface shows through and becomes part of the picture

styles.name: Saharan and San Rock Art
styles.blurb: Across the Sahara and southern Africa, hunter-gatherers painted on sandstone shelters for thousands of years. The figures are elongated and weightless, painted in sun-baked ochres, recording hunts, herds and ceremonies on open rock faces.
look: Long, stretched ochre figures float across pale sandstone
Giraffes and hunters share the same sun-bleached surface
The pigment looks dried and faded by centuries of desert light

styles.name: Mesopotamian Art
styles.tag: Assyrian relief and the Ishtar Gate
styles.blurb: In ancient Iraq, Assyrian kings covered palace walls with carved stone reliefs of processions, hunts and battles, while Babylon's gates gleamed with glazed blue brick and animal reliefs. Everything marches in strict profile — power shown as endless, orderly repetition.
look: She processes in profile between striding lions, like a palace relief come to life
Carved alabaster tones sit beside deep lapis-blue glazed brick
Figures overlap in a flat, rhythmic line with no deep space

styles.name: Cycladic Figures
styles.blurb: Five thousand years ago, sculptors on the Cyclades islands carved white marble figures so reduced and abstract they look like modern art. Arms fold across the belly, the head tilts back like a lyre, and all detail is smoothed away.
look: Her whole form is simplified to folded arms and a lyre-shaped head
Smooth white marble with almost no surface detail
The pose is still, frontal and strangely modern-looking

styles.name: Minoan Fresco
styles.blurb: The Minoans of Crete painted palace walls with joyful, flowing scenes — athletes leaping over bulls, dolphins, lilies — in earthy reds, blues and yellows on plaster. Figures have pinched wasp waists, long curls and a sense of movement no Egyptian artist would allow.
look: A wasp-waisted figure leaps in profile among lilies and dolphins
Earthy reds and blues flow across a pale plaster ground
Curving, springy lines make everything feel mid-motion

styles.name: Etruscan Tomb Painting
styles.blurb: The Etruscans of pre-Roman Italy painted their underground tombs with banquets, dancers and musicians in flat, cheerful colors — a party meant to last forever. The style is decorative and lively, with dark outlines and patterned borders framing the fun.
look: A banquet scene unfolds with dancers and musicians along the wall
Flat, gay colors sit inside confident dark outlines
Patterned bands and small trees divide the wall into scenes

styles.name: Classical Greek Sculpture
styles.blurb: Greek sculptors of the 5th century BCE worked out how a body balances: weight on one leg, hips and shoulders tilting in answer — a relaxed stance called contrapposto. Their marble gods and athletes look calm, ideal and perfectly proportioned, as if good posture were a moral quality.
look: She stands in contrapposto, weight shifted onto one leg
Drapery clings like wet cloth, revealing the body beneath
The marble face is serene and idealized, on a museum plinth

styles.name: Roman Wall Painting
styles.blurb: Wealthy Romans had their villa walls painted with fake architecture, garden views and little floating mythological scenes, all on rich Pompeian red. Buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE, whole rooms survived — painting used as wallpaper, window and daydream at once.
look: She sits inside a painted garden illusion that pretends the wall opens outdoors
Deep red walls frame the scene like a stage set
Small mythological vignettes float in panels around her

styles.name: Roman Mosaic
styles.blurb: Roman floors were pictures built from thousands of tiny stone cubes called tesserae, pressed into mortar. Up close it is rubble; step back and the image snaps together — the original pixel art, framed by black-and-white braided borders.
look: The whole café scene is built from small stone cubes
A black-and-white guilloche braid runs around the border
Colors are the muted tones of real stone, slightly uneven

styles.name: Achaemenid Relief
styles.blurb: At Persepolis, the Persian Empire carved its own portrait in stone: endless lines of tribute-bearers from every subject nation climbing the palace stairs in profile, each gift and costume recorded. Nobody rushes; empire is shown as a queue that never ends.
look: An endless profile procession climbs a carved staircase
She carries a wafer as her tribute among the bearers
Every figure is the same height, in the same measured rhythm

styles.name: Fayum Mummy Portraits
styles.blurb: In Roman Egypt, portraits were painted in hot wax — encaustic — on wooden panels and set into mummies. They are startlingly lifelike: huge dark eyes, individual faces, gold wreaths, painted nearly two thousand years before photography.
look: Huge dark eyes dominate a lifelike, individualized face
A gold wreath catches light against the warm skin tones
The portrait sits on a wood panel shaped to a mummy's curve

styles.name: Early Christian Catacomb Painting
styles.blurb: The first Christian art was painted in underground burial tunnels in Rome: simple, faded frescoes of symbols — fish, anchors, doves — and praying figures with raised arms. It is deliberately humble art, more sign language than spectacle.
look: A simple figure prays with arms raised in the orant pose
Fish and anchor motifs repeat as quiet symbols
Faded pigment sinks into rough, damaged plaster

styles.name: Byzantine Icon
styles.blurb: Byzantine icons are sacred portraits on gold: flat, frontal and solemn, meant as windows into heaven rather than pictures of earth. Space runs backwards — inverse perspective opens toward the viewer — and gold light replaces sunlight.
look: A frontal, solemn figure floats on a flat gold ground
The halo is tooled and punched into the gold
Fine pale highlights model the face in egg-tempera strokes

styles.name: Carolingian and Ottonian Art
styles.blurb: Around the year 1000, the Ottonian emperors commissioned Gospel books with miniatures of enthroned, wide-eyed rulers and saints in jeweled gold frames. Figures are flat and hieratic — all authority and stare, drapery reduced to decorative pattern.
look: An enthroned figure sits inside a jeweled gold frame
Wide, staring eyes carry the whole expression
Drapery falls in flat, repeating decorative patterns

styles.name: Insular Art
styles.blurb: Monks in Ireland and northern Britain filled Gospel books like the Book of Kells with pages of interlace — knotwork ribbons, spiral patterns and beasts biting their own tails. Letters themselves become mazes: her initial is swallowed by the ornament.
look: Her initial letter dissolves into interlacing ribbon patterns
Knotwork beasts weave through carpet-page geometry
Dense ornament covers every corner of the page

styles.name: Romanesque
styles.blurb: Romanesque art served the heavy stone churches of medieval Europe: squat carved figures over doorways, solemn manuscript saints, everything patterned and a little stiff. Drapery is drawn in rhythmic lines, and bodies bend to fit the architecture around them.
look: Squat, solemn carved forms sit under round arches
Drapery is patterned with repeated carved lines
Figures stretch or squeeze to fit the stone frame

styles.name: Gothic and International Gothic
styles.blurb: By 1400, courts across Europe shared one elegant style: figures swaying in an S-curve, jewel-bright colors, and gold backgrounds tooled with tiny punched patterns. It is aristocratic and decorative — painting as embroidery and jewelry combined.
look: An elegant figure sways in a gentle S-curve
The gold background is tooled with fine punched patterns
Jewel colors — deep blue, red and green — glow against the gold

styles.name: Russian Icon
styles.blurb: Russian icon painters like Andrei Rublev made figures weightless and elongated, their faces luminous with quiet joy. Thin lines of gold, called assiste, sparkle on the robes — light itself drawn onto the paint.
look: An elongated figure seems to float rather than stand
The face glows with soft, luminous modeling
Fine gold assiste lines highlight the folds of the robes

styles.name: Ethiopian Christian Painting
styles.blurb: Ethiopian churches are covered with murals of saints and angels, all with enormous almond-shaped eyes, in flat reds, ochres and greens. Painted in rows on church walls, the style stayed proudly local while Ethiopia kept its ancient Christian tradition.
look: Huge almond eyes dominate every face in the scene
Flat reds and ochres fill the wall in bands
She stands in a row of saints, holding a wafer

styles.name: Armenian Manuscripts
styles.blurb: Armenian monks illuminated Gospel books with some of the most intense color in medieval art: deep mineral blues and reds, canon tables under horseshoe arches, and margins alive with birds and flowers. Every page is dense, jeweled and architectural.
look: Canon-table arches frame the page like a little building
Birds and flowers crowd the margins
Intense mineral color — deep blue and red — fills every area

styles.name: Islamic Calligraphy
styles.blurb: Because Islamic tradition avoids images of sacred figures, calligraphy — beautiful writing — became the highest visual art. In flowing thuluth script, letters stretch, stack and interlace until words become architecture, and here her silhouette is formed by the letterforms themselves.
look: Her silhouette is built entirely from flowing black and gold letters
Letterforms stretch and stack like architecture on ivory paper
There are no pictures — the writing is the image

styles.name: Arabesque and Geometric Pattern
styles.blurb: Islamic ornament weaves two systems together: scrolling plant tendrils that never end, and exact geometry of stars and polygons fitted without gaps. The pattern has no beginning, center or edge — an image of infinity you can tile across a whole building.
look: Her figure is woven into interlacing vegetal scrolls
Eight-point stars lock into the geometry around her
The pattern repeats with no visible start or finish

styles.name: Ottoman Miniature
styles.blurb: Ottoman court painters documented the sultan's world in miniatures with a flattened, bird's-eye view: palaces, ceremonies and sieges laid out like patterned maps. Tiny figures in bright clothes act out history inside tiled courtyards, with no shadows and no single viewpoint.
look: A flat bird's-eye palace scene spreads out like a map
Tiny patterned figures fill the courtyards and rooms
She serves coffee in a tiled kiosk at the center

styles.name: Qajar Painting
styles.blurb: Qajar Persia's court portraits show kings and beauties frontally, with joined arched eyebrows, huge eyes, jeweled crowns and sashes, against flat decorative backdrops. Part painting, part jewelry display — oil paint used with a miniaturist's love of ornament.
look: Arched, joined eyebrows and large eyes define the face
A jeweled crown and sash glitter against the flat backdrop
The frontal courtly pose is stiff, symmetrical and decorative

lessons.title: World Traditions II: Asia
lessons.bigIdea: Asia's picture traditions prize the brush, the scroll and the miniature page — and often leave emptiness to do half the talking.
lessons.intro: From Ajanta's cave murals and Rajput miniatures to Chinese literati landscapes, Japanese gold screens and Korean folk painting, this lesson crosses the continent. Watch how ink behaves differently in every hand, how gold stands in for light and air, and how a tiny figure in a vast landscape can carry the whole meaning.
lessons.exercise: Find the picture with the most empty space. What is the emptiness doing — sky, silence, spirit, or all three?

styles.name: Mughal Album Painting
styles.blurb: Persian technique meets Indian observation at the Mughal court: exquisitely fine miniatures, mounted in albums with floral borders, recording court life, hunts and nature with jewelers' precision.
look: Hair-thin lines model faces and fabrics
A wide floral margin frames the scene
Colors are soft jewels — refined, never loud

styles.name: Mithila Painting
styles.tag: Madhubani folk art, India and Nepal
styles.blurb: Painted by women of Mithila on walls and paper for weddings and festivals: double outlines, hatched color fills, and no empty space anywhere — nature abhors a vacuum here.
look: Every area is filled with pattern or creatures
Double outlines give shapes a stitched energy
Faces often appear in profile with one large eye

styles.name: Rinpa
styles.blurb: Rinpa artists distilled nature into design: gold-leaf grounds, bold silhouettes of plum, maple and waves, and tarashikomi — pigments pooled wet into each other for soft, lucky edges.
look: Gold ground replaces sky and air
Natural motifs are simplified into emblems
Pooled pigment blurs some edges on purpose

styles.name: Chinese Ink Landscape
styles.blurb: For a thousand years, China's scholar-painters held landscape — shan shui, 'mountain-water' — as the highest art. Our model keeps a seat, but the café becomes a pavilion among cliffs, mist and waterfalls: humans are guests in nature, not its owners.
look: Mist and empty paper do as much work as ink
Mountains stack in receding veils
The figure is small inside a vast world

styles.name: Chaekgeori
styles.blurb: Joseon-dynasty screens celebrating scholarship: books, brushes, ceramics and curios stacked on shelves in playful near-trompe-l'œil. A still life that is really a portrait of a mind.
look: Shelves of books and objects fill the picture
Objects are painted with loving, slightly impossible precision
Our model sits inside the library like one of its treasures

styles.name: Kalighat Painting
styles.blurb: Painters outside Kolkata's Kalighat temple sold quick, bold watercolors to pilgrims: sweeping single-stroke outlines, flat washes, figures modeled with a few confident shadows. A souvenir that became a school.
look: One sweeping brush line defines each form
Flat washes with minimal shading
The figure feels sculptural despite the flatness

styles.name: Wayang Kulit
styles.blurb: The picture is a shadow: a perforated leather puppet, gilded and painted, performed behind a lit screen with rods at its joints. You are seeing the puppet itself — profile is not a style here, it is physics.
look: The figure is a flat silhouette with pierced patterns
Articulated rods attach at the joints
Warm flame-light glows behind the screen

styles.name: Ajanta Murals
styles.blurb: Painted over 1,500 years ago inside rock-cut caves in India, the Ajanta murals tell Buddhist stories with soft, shaded bodies and warm earth colors. Nothing is outlined harshly — forms melt out of the dark like figures in candlelight. Here she appears as a graceful attendant among lotus ponds.
look: Figures are modeled with soft shading, not hard outlines
The palette is all earth pigments — ochre, rust, green and brown
Lotus ponds and lush plants fill the space around her

styles.name: Rajput and Pahari Miniature
styles.blurb: In the royal courts of Rajasthan, artists painted tiny, jewel-like scenes of love, music and monsoon romance, often small enough to hold in one hand. The colors are flat and hot, and every leaf and cloud is drawn with a hair-thin brush. Our scene becomes a lovers'-meeting on a terrace under storm clouds.
look: Flat, saturated color laid down like enamel
Fine brush lines pick out jewelry, leaves and patterned cloth
Dark monsoon clouds press in above the terrace scene

styles.name: Tibetan Thangka
styles.blurb: A thangka is a Tibetan Buddhist scroll painting, made to be rolled up, carried, and unrolled for teaching and meditation. A calm central deity sits inside a palace of perfect symmetry, ringed by clouds, mountains and smaller figures. Here she takes the deity's seat, enthroned at the center of the mandala.
look: Perfect symmetry around her enthroned figure
Mineral blues and greens with fine gold outlines
Stylized cloud bands and tiny landscapes fill every corner

styles.name: Chola Bronze
styles.blurb: A thousand years ago, sculptors of the Chola dynasty in south India cast temple gods in bronze using the lost-wax method, pouring metal into a mold that is destroyed to free the figure. The results are dark, polished and impossibly graceful. She becomes a dancing deity in the famous tribhanga pose — body curved in three bends — inside a ring of flame.
look: Dark polished bronze with a soft golden sheen
Her body curves in the three-bend tribhanga pose
A ring of carved flames frames the dancing figure

styles.name: Pattachitra
styles.blurb: Pattachitra means 'picture on cloth' — painters in Odisha, India, still prepare cotton canvas with chalk and gum, then crowd it with stories of gods and heroes. Every figure gets a bold outline and a flat field of color, usually a blazing red background. She stands at the center of a dense mythological crowd.
look: Bold black outlines around every figure
A flat, intense red background
The crowd is packed edge to edge with story figures

styles.name: Warli
styles.blurb: Warli artists in Maharashtra paint with white rice paste on walls of red mud, using the simplest possible figures — two triangles joined at the tip make a person. Whole villages of these stick figures dance, harvest and celebrate in spirals and rows. Here she joins the tarpa dance, reduced to the same joyful geometry as everyone else.
look: People are built from two joined triangles
White rice-paste figures on a red-ochre wall
Dancers link hands in a great spiral around a musician

styles.name: Gond Art
styles.blurb: The Gond people of central India have a painting tradition where surfaces come alive with pattern — a figure's body might be built entirely from tiny dots and dashes. Peacocks, deer and trees of life glow in saturated color against dark grounds. In this version, her whole figure is assembled from that dotted texture.
look: Her figure is built from thousands of dots and dashes
Peacocks and trees of life in saturated, glowing color
Pattern covers everything — no surface is left plain

styles.name: Tanjore Painting
styles.blurb: Tanjore painting, from Tamil Nadu in south India, is devotional art that literally sparkles: artists build up a figure on a wooden panel, then decorate it with real gold foil and inset glass beads. The result is icon-like, frontal and rich, meant to be worshipped as much as looked at. She poses like a temple deity, gilded and gleaming.
look: Real-looking gold foil covers jewelry and clothing
Tiny glass gems are inset like jewels in a crown
A frontal, icon-like pose against deep red tones

styles.name: Kalamkari
styles.blurb: Kalamkari is cloth painted by hand with a bamboo pen, using dyes made from plants and minerals — the word means 'pen work'. Huge temple cloths told epic stories in panels, so worshippers could read the cloth like a comic strip. Our version frames her story in narrative border panels, all in those warm natural-dye colors.
look: Fine bamboo-pen outlines with a slightly trembling hand-drawn feel
Muted natural-dye colors — indigo, rust, mustard, leaf green
Story panels run along the borders like a frame

styles.name: Company Painting
styles.blurb: When British East India Company officials wanted records of India, they hired Indian artists, who blended their miniature-painting skill with European watercolor naturalism. The results are precise, calm catalogues of costumes, trades, plants and tools. Here she is documented like a specimen, her equipment and trade arranged neatly around her.
look: Precise watercolor detail, almost like a scientific record
Her tools and trade objects are catalogued around her
A plain, pale background keeps the focus on documentation

styles.name: Bengal School
styles.blurb: In the early 1900s, Abanindranath Tagore and his circle rejected slick academic painting and revived a misty, poetic Indian style, borrowing the wash technique from Japanese artists. Figures dissolve into foggy, muted color — painting as memory or dream rather than report. She drifts through this one like a figure in a half-remembered story.
look: The figure is misty and soft-edged, as if seen through fog
Muted, washed-out color with very few hard lines
A dreamy, melancholic mood hangs over the scene

styles.name: Khmer Relief
styles.blurb: The temples of Angkor in Cambodia are wrapped in bas-reliefs — shallow carvings that cover entire walls with dancers, battles and cosmic myths. Apsaras, heavenly dancers, twist gracefully among crowds drawn from the great churning-of-the-ocean legend. Here she is carved as one of them, her café-scene identity translated into lichen-softened sandstone.
look: Shallow carved stone with softened, weathered edges
She dances as an apsara among a carved crowd
Traces of lichen and age mottle the sandstone surface

styles.name: Thai Temple Mural
styles.blurb: Thai temple walls are covered with murals of the Ramakien, the national epic of kings, monkeys and demons, painted in flat perspective with black lacquer and gold. Every inch teems with palaces, battles and festivals at once. She takes her place in a pavilion scene inside that golden crowd.
look: Gold flecks and gold leaf glitter across the surface
Crowded epic scenes fill the wall with no empty space
Flat perspective — palaces and people stack upward instead of receding

styles.name: Balinese Kamasan Painting
styles.blurb: Kamasan painting, from one village in Bali, retells Hindu epics on cloth using the visual language of shadow-puppet theatre. Figures appear in the puppet-like profile called ringgit, and separate episodes are divided by flames, trees and rocks. Our café scene is split into episodes across the cloth, puppet-style.
look: Figures are drawn in stiff shadow-puppet profile
Episodes are separated by flames, trees and rock shapes
The whole story unfolds on one crowded cloth

styles.name: Đông Hồ Prints
styles.blurb: Đông Hồ prints are folk woodblocks made for the Lunar New Year in one Vietnamese village, printed with natural colors on paper coated with crushed shell, which gives it a pearly shimmer. The images are bold, cheerful wishes for luck and prosperity. Here the café becomes a festive village scene in that bold-outlined style.
look: Bold black outlines with flat natural colors inside
A pearly shell-white shimmer on the paper
A cheerful festival mood — this is a good-luck picture

styles.name: Vietnamese Lacquer Painting
styles.blurb: Sơn mài is Vietnam's modern lacquer painting: artists build up many layers of deep red, black and gold lacquer, sometimes with eggshell inlaid, then polish and sand the surface until images glow out of the darkness. It is painting that behaves like polished wood and candlelight at once. Her figure emerges slowly from the dark ground.
look: Deep red, black and gold layers with a polished glow
Her figure emerges out of darkness rather than sitting on a background
Highlights gleam like light on varnished wood

styles.name: Chinese Calligraphy
styles.blurb: In China, calligraphy is considered the highest art of all — the way a brush moves reveals the writer's energy and character, and a single stroke can hold speed, pressure and breath. Running script flows like water, each stroke leaning into the next. Here her whole silhouette is suggested by one sweeping calligraphic gesture.
look: Her silhouette is formed by one sweeping brush gesture
Ink shades shift from black to pale gray inside single strokes
A small red seal stamp balances the composition

styles.name: Gongbi Court Painting
styles.blurb: Gongbi means 'meticulous brush' — the polished court style of imperial China, where artists drew fine ink outlines on silk and filled them with thin layers of mineral color. It is the opposite of splashy: patient, exact and luxurious. She becomes a court lady among peonies, holding her wafer with the care usually reserved for a fan or flower.
look: Hair-fine ink outlines filled with delicate mineral color
Peonies and court details are rendered petal by petal
A smooth silk surface with a soft, even sheen

styles.name: Literati Painting
styles.blurb: China's scholar-officials painted for themselves, not for sale, and prized personal expression over professional polish — a few dry, scratchy brushstrokes could say more than a finished picture. Their landscapes are mostly emptiness, with a tiny human figure lost in the vastness. She is that tiny figure, seated in a pavilion under huge empty silk.
look: Sparse dry-brush strokes with lots of visible paper texture
Vast empty silk surrounds one very small figure
A blank space is left for a poem or inscription — the colophon

styles.name: Dunhuang Buddhist Murals
styles.blurb: The Mogao caves at Dunhuang, on the Silk Road in China, hold centuries of Buddhist murals in brilliant mineral blue and green. Their most beloved figures are apsaras — flying spirits who float weightlessly, ribbons streaming, scattering flowers. Our version turns the café into a cave paradise, with apsaras circling around her on aged, cracked plaster.
look: Flying apsaras with long ribbons swirl around the scene
Mineral blue-green color against warm aged plaster
Cracks and flaking show the wall's great age

styles.name: Chinese Ritual Bronzes
styles.blurb: Over 3,000 years ago, Shang and Zhou dynasty craftsmen cast huge bronze vessels for rituals — tripods called ding, covered in swirling patterns and taotie, a mysterious animal-mask face. Time has turned the metal green with patina. Here she stands among the vessels as a taotie-masked figure, part of that ancient bronze world.
look: Green patina crusts the dark bronze surfaces
Taotie animal-mask patterns repeat in bands
Massive tripod ding vessels anchor the composition

styles.name: Shanghai School
styles.blurb: In the booming port city of Shanghai in the late 1800s, painters like Ren Bonian loosened up traditional ink painting — splashier brushwork, brighter color, subjects from modern city life. It was ink painting learning to keep up with a fast, commercial city. She gets that treatment here: bold strokes, flowers, and a modern city girl's energy.
look: Bold, splashy ink-and-color brushwork
Bright flowers painted with loose, wet strokes
A lively modern energy replaces courtly restraint

styles.name: Lingnan School
styles.blurb: The Lingnan School, founded in Canton (Guangzhou) in the early 1900s, deliberately fused Chinese ink with Western watercolor and Japanese techniques — its founders called it a revolution in painting. Figures glow with atmospheric light and drift in clouds of color. Here her ink figure is washed with that luminous, modern light.
look: Ink drawing softened by watercolor light and shadow
Clouds of atmospheric color wash across the scene
A freshness that mixes Chinese, Western and Japanese habits

styles.name: Contemporary Ink
styles.blurb: Today's ink artists push the oldest medium in Asia into new territory — ink poured by the bucket, scanned, glitched, or spread across whole walls. The tradition is treated as a living material, not a museum piece. In this version, huge abstract ink fields and digital glitches surround her small figure standing in the wash.
look: Huge abstract fields of pooled and splashed ink
Digital glitch streaks cut through the traditional wash
Her small figure stands inside the ink rather than before it

styles.name: Yamato-e Handscrolls
styles.blurb: Yamato-e is Japan's classical painting style, used for handscrolls that unroll scene by scene like a slow film. A famous trick is the 'blown-off roof' view, which peeks into palace rooms from above while bands of gold cloud separate one episode from the next. Our café becomes a court interior seen through that missing roof.
look: A blown-off-roof view looks down into the room
Bands of gold cloud divide the story into episodes
Small faces are drawn with fine, minimal ink lines

styles.name: Kanō School Screens
styles.blurb: The Kanō school supplied Japan's shoguns and castles for centuries with bold folding screens: powerful pine trees, hawks and tigers painted against backgrounds of pure gold leaf. The gold is not decoration — it reflects light and makes the room glow. Here she sits in a castle room scene spread across folding panels, backed by that golden field.
look: A background of flat, glowing gold leaf
Bold pine branches and a hawk painted with strong brushwork
Folding panel divisions cut vertical seams through the scene

styles.name: Zen Ink Painting
styles.blurb: Zen monks painted with ink as a form of meditation: a picture made in one breath, with no corrections, values emptiness as much as the strokes themselves. The most famous image is the ensō, a single circular brushstroke left slightly open. In this version her figure is drawn in one breath beside an ensō, surrounded by white silence.
look: One-breath brushstrokes that cannot hide corrections
A single open ensō circle floats in the space
Most of the picture is empty white — the silence is the subject

styles.name: Nihonga
styles.blurb: When Japan modernized in the late 1800s, painters created Nihonga — 'Japanese-style painting' — to keep traditional materials alive: mineral pigments ground from stone, gold leaf, silk supports, soft graded washes. It is traditional technique deliberately carried into the modern age. She appears in those glowing minerals, with cranes and pine for company.
look: Grainy mineral pigments with a soft, stony glow
Gold leaf and silk give the surface a quiet shimmer
Cranes and pine share the scene in soft graded washes

styles.name: Nanga
styles.blurb: Nanga was Japan's version of the scholar-amateur style: loose, playful ink landscapes painted by poets and intellectuals rather than professionals. The ideal subject is a recluse in a mountain hut, far from ambition and noise. Here she plays that recluse, taking her café break in a hut among sketchy peaks.
look: Loose, dry brushwork with a sketchy, playful feel
Light color tints wash over the ink lines
A tiny hut and recluse figure nestle in a big landscape

styles.name: Sōsaku-hanga
styles.blurb: Sōsaku-hanga, Japan's 'creative print' movement, insisted the artist do everything — draw, carve and print alone — treating the woodblock like a personal diary rather than a factory product. The cuts are bold and expressive, gouge marks proudly visible. Our café scene is carved in that spirit, rough edges and all.
look: Bold carved blocks with visible gouge marks
Rough, expressive edges instead of polished finish
Strong black-and-color contrasts from the hand-cut wood

styles.name: Mingei Folk Craft
styles.blurb: Mingei means 'folk craft' — a Japanese movement that found beauty in humble, handmade everyday objects made by unknown craftsmen: rough pottery, woven cloth, wooden bowls. Perfection was the enemy; warmth and use were the point. Here the star is her café cup itself, reimagined as a rustic Mashiko stoneware piece among indigo textiles.
look: A rustic, slightly irregular stoneware cup takes center stage
Deep indigo textiles with simple woven patterns
Surfaces look handmade and well-used, not machine-perfect

styles.name: Minhwa Folk Painting
styles.blurb: Minhwa is Korean folk painting — bright, humorous pictures made by ordinary people for luck, health and laughter. Its most famous scene pairs a foolish tiger with a clever magpie, a gentle joke at the expense of the powerful. In this version she joins that world as the smiling scholar, in flat bright color.
look: Flat, bright folk colors with simple bold shapes
A tiger-and-magpie pairing brings the traditional joke along
Her scholar figure smiles with unpretentious charm

styles.name: True-View Landscape
styles.blurb: In the 1700s, the Korean painter Jeong Seon rejected copied Chinese scenery and painted Korea's actual mountains — especially its dramatic granite peaks — with bold, slashing brushwork. The style is called 'true-view' because the place is real and recognizable. She walks tiny on a path below those unmistakable peaks.
look: Granite peaks built from bold, energetic brush slashes
The landscape is a real, recognizable Korean mountain
Her figure is tiny on a path, dwarfed by the rock

styles.name: Goryeo Buddhist Painting
