styles.blurb: The Goryeo dynasty of Korea (918–1392) produced some of the most delicate Buddhist paintings in the world — silk icons of Kannon, the bodhisattva of compassion, drawn with lines fine as hair and dusted with gold powder. Only about 160 survive. Here the graceful water-moon Kannon composition gains her as an attendant.
look: Hair-fine lines and translucent silk drapery
Gold powder detail glitters on robes and halos
A calm water-moon composition of perfect stillness

styles.name: Dansaekhwa
styles.blurb: Dansaekhwa, 'monochrome painting', emerged in 1970s Korea: artists pushed, dragged and soaked paint into canvas through repeated physical actions, usually in a single color. The painting is the record of a process — meditation you can see. Here her figure barely emerges from a field of pushed white paint.
look: One color only — a field of worked white paint
Texture records the pushing and dragging of the process
Her figure emerges faintly, like something remembered

lessons.title: World Traditions III: Africa, Oceania and the Americas
lessons.bigIdea: Cloth, bark, feathers, clay and carved wood are picture surfaces too — and many of these traditions never separated 'art' from ceremony, story and daily life.
lessons.intro: Benin bronzes and Kuba cloth from Africa; dot fields and bark paintings from Aboriginal Australia; Māori carving and tapa cloth from the Pacific; Aztec codices, Andean textiles, ledger drawings and pottery from the Americas. Notice how often the image is something you wear, carry, unroll or walk around — not a rectangle on a wall.
lessons.exercise: Pick one work and name the job it does besides looking good: remembering, warning, honoring, teaching, protecting. How does its material help it do that job?

styles.name: Classic Maya Painted Ceramics
styles.blurb: Maya artists painted palace scenes and myths around cylindrical vases in a calligraphic line, with glyph blocks that actually write names and events — pictures and text in one band.
look: The scene unrolls like a scroll around the pot
Cream, red and black carry the palette
Glyph blocks sit inside the picture as captions

styles.name: Ayacucho Retablo
styles.blurb: Andean artists pack whole worlds into wooden boxes: tiers of small painted figures acting out festivals, markets and daily life behind opening doors. Our café joins a fab scene inside the box.
look: The scene lives inside an open wooden box
Small modeled figures, brightly painted
Multiple tiers tell several stories at once

styles.name: Nok Terracotta
styles.blurb: The Nok culture of what is now Nigeria made some of Africa's oldest surviving sculptures: lifelike heads fired from clay over 2,000 years ago. Here her portrait becomes one of those terracotta heads, all earthy red-brown surface and calm, stylized features.
look: Pierced, almond-shaped eyes stare through the clay
An elaborate coiffure of buns and braids crowns the head
The surface is matte, earthy terracotta with a fired roughness

styles.name: Ife and Benin Bronzes
styles.blurb: The kingdoms of Ife and Benin cast bronze with a lost-wax technique so refined that early European visitors refused to believe it was local work. Our picture follows the Benin palace plaques: a flat relief in dark metal where she stands in court regalia among warriors.
look: Everything is modeled in dark, polished cast bronze
Figures are arranged in a flat relief, like a palace plaque
Warriors and Portuguese soldiers flank her in the background

styles.name: African Carved Masks
styles.blurb: Across West and Central Africa, masks are not decorations but presences — worn in dances, kept as reliquaries, used to mediate with ancestors. This gallery re-carves her face twice: once as a pale Fang reliquary head, once as a dark Dan mask.
look: One version of her face is coated in white kaolin clay
The other is polished dark wood with narrow, serene features
Both masks simplify her likeness into smooth, sculptural planes

styles.name: Kuba Cloth
styles.blurb: The Kuba kingdom of the Congo built an entire design culture from raffia palm fiber — embroidered, appliquéd and cut-pile cloth covered in bold, improvisational geometry. Here her silhouette sits inside that pattern world, woven rather than drawn.
look: Interlocking geometric shapes fill every corner of the cloth
The palette stays earthy: browns, tans and black
Her figure appears as a flat silhouette inside the pattern

styles.name: Kente
styles.blurb: Kente is woven on a loom in narrow strips, then sewn together into cloths of alternating patterned blocks — and each pattern has a name and a meaning. In this version the whole portrait is a weaving: her figure emerges from bright bands of gold, green, red and black geometry.
look: Narrow horizontal strips alternate between different patterns
Colors are saturated and jewel-bright
Her figure is built from the same geometric blocks as the cloth

styles.name: Ndebele House Painting
styles.blurb: Ndebele women in South Africa paint their house walls with huge, crisp geometric murals — a public art of identity, renewed for ceremonies and celebrations. She stands before one of those walls, wearing the beaded apron and ornaments of Ndebele dress.
look: Every shape on the wall is outlined in thick black
Flat blocks of blue, yellow, red and green stack in bold geometry
Her beaded apron echoes the wall's patterns in miniature

styles.name: Adire
styles.blurb: Adire is the Yoruba art of indigo resist dyeing: patterns are painted or stenciled in cassava paste, and the cloth is dipped in indigo so the pasted areas stay white. The result here is a two-tone world — her figure and café motifs floating white on deep blue.
look: Only two colors appear: white and deep indigo blue
Fine crackle lines run through the dyed areas where the paste broke
Cups and café motifs repeat as small white pattern units

styles.name: Uli and Nsibidi
styles.blurb: Uli is the Igbo art of elegant curving line, traditionally painted on walls and bodies; nsibidi is a related system of ideogram signs. Together they turn her figure into calligraphy — a body described by a few sweeping black strokes on a whitewashed wall.
look: Her form is drawn with a few long, sweeping black curves
Small nsibidi ideogram signs punctuate the white space
The background stays bare whitewash, like a freshly plastered wall

styles.name: Asafo Flags
styles.blurb: Fante asafo companies in Ghana carry appliqué flags that picture proverbs — a boast, a warning or a joke told in flat cloth figures. In this flag she is the hero of the scene, holding a wafer aloft like a company standard.
look: Figures are flat appliqué shapes with hard, cut edges
She holds a wafer standard high at the center of the scene
Bright, clashing cloth colors fill the rectangular banner

styles.name: Tingatinga
styles.blurb: Tingatinga began in 1960s Tanzania with Edward Said Tingatinga, who painted animals in bicycle enamel on masonite board. The style stuck: glossy, flat, saturated pictures of animals and everyday life. Here she joins a cheerful crowd of oversized animals.
look: The paint looks glossy, like enamel on a hard board
Animals are big, flat and brightly colored with tiny pattern details
Everyone faces forward in a cheerful, crowded composition

styles.name: Oshogbo School
styles.blurb: In 1960s Oshogbo, Nigeria, the organizer Ulli Beier encouraged untrained local artists to paint their Yoruba spirit world in a free, experimental way. The result mixes printmaking textures with dense crowds of spirits, animals and people — and she stands in the middle of the swirl.
look: Lizard and animal motifs repeat across the surface like a pattern
Spirit figures crowd and swirl densely around her
Lines and textures feel half-printed, half-painted

styles.name: El Anatsui's Metal Tapestries
styles.blurb: Ghanaian artist El Anatsui stitches thousands of discarded bottle caps and seals into vast metal hangings that drape like cloth. Her portrait here is built the same way — a shimmering mosaic of tiny metal pieces that folds and ripples.
look: Thousands of tiny bottle seals tile the surface like chain mail
The hanging drapes in soft folds despite being metal
Gold, silver and copper tones shimmer across her portrait

styles.name: Aboriginal Bark Painting
styles.blurb: In Arnhem Land, Aboriginal artists paint clan designs on sheets of eucalyptus bark, filling forms with rarrk — fine cross-hatched lines that make the surface shimmer. Her figure and even a coffee cup are painted as clan motifs in ochres on bark.
look: Fine cross-hatching (rarrk) fills the inside of every form
The background is the rough brown of real bark
Colors are earth ochres: white, yellow, red and black

styles.name: Western Desert Dot Painting
styles.blurb: The Papunya painting movement of the 1970s turned Aboriginal desert knowledge into acrylic on canvas: maps seen from above, drawn in dots. This one charts her journey to the café as concentric meeting-places joined by dotted travel lines.
look: Concentric circles mark places, like sites on a map
Dotted lines trace a journey between the circles
The whole scene is seen from directly above, in desert ochres

styles.name: Māori Carving and Kōwhaiwhai
styles.tag: New Zealand wood and rafter art
styles.blurb: Māori whakairo carving covers meeting-house posts and panels with koru spirals unfurling like fern fronds, while kōwhaiwhai patterns paint the rafters above in red, black and white. Her figure is carved into that wooden world, spiral within spiral.
look: Koru spirals curl through her carved figure and the background
The figure is relief-carved wood, not flat paint
Rafter patterns repeat in strict red, black and white

styles.name: Tapa Cloth
styles.blurb: Across the Pacific, cloth is made by beating tree bark into soft sheets, then stamping or stenciling them with geometric designs. In this tapa her figure becomes a motif, repeated across the cloth like a stamp in a pattern.
look: Her figure repeats in rows like a stamped motif
Designs are only brown and black on cream bark fiber
The fibrous, slightly uneven texture of beaten bark shows through

styles.name: Sepik Carving
styles.blurb: Along Papua New Guinea's Sepik River, carvers cover spirit boards and house posts with bold swirling faces, crocodiles and ancestor figures. She appears among them in a carved board, picked out in ochre, white and black paint.
look: Faces are built from bold swirls, hooks and concentric circles
Crocodile and ancestor motifs crowd around her figure
Paint is limited to ochre red, white and black on carved wood

styles.name: Rapa Nui
styles.blurb: Rapa Nui — Easter Island — is famous for the moai, giant stone heads with long torsos, and for rongorongo, an undeciphered script carved on wood. At dawn she stands small before the statues, a reminder of how the island's art dwarfs any single person.
look: The moai tower over her, huge-headed and solemn
A wooden tablet nearby carries rows of tiny carved glyphs
Dawn light rakes across the stone and the grassy slope

styles.name: Hawaiian Featherwork
styles.blurb: Hawaiian chiefs wore ʻahu ʻula — cloaks and capes of thousands of tiny red and yellow feathers tied to fiber netting, among the most precious objects in the islands. Her portrait is rendered in that feather geometry, glowing like royalty.
look: The surface is made of tiny overlapping feather tufts
Bold crescents and triangles pattern the red and yellow field
The edges show the fine netting the feathers are tied to

styles.name: Olmec Sculpture
styles.blurb: The Olmec, Mesoamerica's earliest great culture, carved basalt boulders into colossal heads up to three meters tall. Here one of those heads wears her features and glasses, with a small baby-face figurine beside it in a jungle clearing.
look: Her face is carved at monumental scale in dark basalt
The head wears a close-fitting carved cap, like the ancient heads
A small pale figurine contrasts with the giant stone head

styles.name: Teotihuacan Murals
styles.blurb: The apartment compounds of Teotihuacan were covered in murals — flat figures in procession against deep red walls, full of butterflies, water and gods. In this mural she joins the procession, offering a wafer before a pyramid.
look: The background is a flat, deep mural red
Priests and butterflies move in a level procession
Figures are outlined and unshaded, like paint on plaster

styles.name: Aztec and Mixtec Codices
styles.blurb: Mixtec and Aztec scribes painted screenfold books of deerskin that record genealogies, conquests and calendars in flat outline figures. On this page she is a named lady in a dynastic scene — the curl at her mouth is a speech scroll, and the signs around her are days of the calendar.
look: Figures are flat, outlined and colored without shading
A curled speech scroll leaves her mouth
Small day-sign glyphs are arranged around the scene

styles.name: Andean Textiles
styles.blurb: In the Andes, weaving was a high technology: Paracas embroiderers and Inca weavers encoded identity in cloth, including tocapu — grids of geometric squares that may have worked like a written language. Her figure is woven into such a grid, in alpaca-wool colors.
look: Her figure is built from a grid of small geometric squares
The wool colors are warm: camel, rust, cream and indigo
An embroidered border of small repeated figures frames the cloth

styles.name: Moche and Nazca Ceramics
styles.blurb: The Moche of Peru's north coast made portrait vessels — ceramic heads so individual they seem to depict real people — with a distinctive stirrup-shaped spout. Her head becomes one: a cream-and-red-brown vessel you could pour from.
look: Her head is the vessel, with a stirrup spout rising behind
Painting is only cream and red-brown slip on clay
The portrait is sculptural and lifelike, not a flat drawing

styles.name: Northwest Coast Formline
styles.blurb: Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast artists build animals and people from a flowing design system called formline: swelling black lines, egg-shaped ovoids and U-forms that split a creature across a surface. Her figure follows the same logic, unfolding in black, red and teal.
look: Thick black formlines swell and taper as they curve
Ovoids and U-shapes form her joints, eyes and features
The figure is split and spread flat, in split-raven fashion

styles.name: Plains Ledger Art
styles.blurb: In the late 1800s, Plains artists drew their histories in the lined pages of account books, using colored pencils and crayons. The blue ledger lines show through the flat, lively scenes — and here she rides through one, coffee cup raised like a lance.
look: Blue ruled lines of the account paper show through the drawing
Figures are flat and brightly colored, with no shading
Horses and riders spread across the page in profile

styles.name: Pueblo Pottery
styles.blurb: A thousand years ago, Mimbres potters in the Southwest painted the insides of bowls with black-on-white animals, people and geometry. This bowl paints her at its center, ringed by feather and stepped patterns, meant to be seen as the bowl empties.
look: The picture lives inside the curve of a bowl
Everything is black paint on a white clay slip
Feather and step motifs ring her central figure

styles.name: Inuit Prints
styles.blurb: At Kinngait (Cape Dorset) in Nunavut, Inuit artists developed stonecut printmaking — bold, simple images cut into stone and printed by hand, made famous by Kenojuak Ashevak's radiant owls. Here she stands among Arctic animals, ulu knife and wafer in hand.
look: Shapes are bold, rounded and almost completely flat
Animals surround her in a balanced, symmetrical arrangement
Ink edges show the slight grain of the stonecut print

styles.name: Navajo Weaving
styles.blurb: Diné (Navajo) weavers create rugs of striking geometry on upright looms; the famous storm pattern links a central rectangle to the four corners with stepped lightning lines. Her figure is woven into that design in red, gray, black and white wool.
look: Stepped, zigzag lines connect the center to the four corners
The palette is strictly red, gray, black and white
Her figure is built from the same angular wool geometry

styles.name: Woodlands School
styles.blurb: Norval Morrisseau, an Anishinaabe artist from Canada, founded the Woodlands School by painting his people's legends in bold black outlines and bright color, with X-ray lines revealing the inner spirit of things. Here flowing lines connect her to the animals around her — everything is joined.
look: Thick black outlines wrap every figure
Inner X-ray lines and dots show bones and spirit inside bodies
Thin flowing lines connect her to birds and animals

styles.name: Huichol Yarn Painting
styles.blurb: Wixárika (Huichol) artists in Mexico make nierika — pictures built by pressing strands of bright yarn into beeswax on a board. Every line of her portrait is a thread, surrounded by the deer, maize and peyote motifs of Wixárika sacred art.
look: Every contour is a visible strand of pressed yarn
Colors are electric: turquoise, magenta, yellow and green
Deer and peyote motifs glow around her figure

styles.name: Amate Painting
styles.blurb: Amate is paper made from beaten tree bark in Mexico, and painters in Guerrero cover it with bright village scenes — fiestas, harvests, markets — in jewel colors on the brown paper. She has a stall at this fiesta, selling wafers among the birds and flowers.
look: The paper itself is warm brown and visibly fibrous
Bright, unmixed colors pop against the bark tone
Birds, flowers and villagers fill every gap in the scene

styles.name: Cuzco School
styles.blurb: In colonial Cuzco, Peru, Indigenous painters fused European religious painting with local taste: flat, patterned surfaces and robes stamped with real gold brocade. She appears as a Madonna-like figure in those gold-flecked robes, with Andean flowers and birds at her feet.
look: Gold stamped patterns glitter across the robes
The figure is flat and frontal, with little interest in depth
Local Andean flowers and small birds fill the foreground

styles.name: Casta Painting
styles.blurb: Eighteenth-century Mexico produced casta paintings — sets of panels cataloguing families of different racial mixtures, each with a written label. Whatever we think of the categories now, the panels are vivid records of colonial daily life: markets, clothes, food. Here she serves coffee in one such labeled market panel.
look: The scene is one tidy panel from a numbered set
A caption label identifies the family, as on the originals
Market goods, clothes and food are itemized in fine detail

styles.name: Haitian Painting
styles.blurb: Haiti's self-taught painters, encouraged by the Centre d'Art in Port-au-Prince from 1944, became famous for lush, Eden-like scenes in flat, brilliant color. In this one she keeps a market stall under almond trees in a green world without shadows or worry.
look: Layered greens build a dense, paradise-like landscape
Figures are flat, bright and evenly lit, with no shadows
Every leaf and fruit is painted with patient, decorative care

styles.name: Mola
styles.blurb: Guna women in Panama sew molas by stacking colored cloth, cutting through the layers and stitching the edges back — reverse appliqué. Her figure is built that way, in cutaway rainbow layers shared with fish and birds.
look: Her figure is formed by cut edges revealing layers beneath
Fine stitched lines outline every cut shape
Rainbow layers repeat in fish, birds and maze-like filler patterns

lessons.title: The Western Canon: Order, Drama and Feeling
lessons.bigIdea: From 1400 to 1900, European painting swung like a pendulum: reason, then emotion, then reason again — each swing reacting to the last.
lessons.intro: Renaissance artists built space with geometry. Baroque artists flooded it with drama. Neoclassicists demanded noble order, Romantics answered with storms and feelings, and Realists pointed at ordinary workers. Walk the pendulum swing by swing and you can read most museum walls in Europe.
lessons.exercise: Stand back from the pictures and sort them into 'calm and ordered' versus 'stormy and emotional'. Does the historical order alternate?

styles.name: Renaissance Perspective
styles.blurb: Brunelleschi and Alberti turned space into mathematics: one vanishing point, receding floor tiles, architecture like a proof. The four variants place our model in loggias, halls and piazzas built by the rule.
look: Floor lines and arches converge to one point
Space feels measurable and calm
Figures are placed like pieces in the geometry

styles.name: Baroque
styles.blurb: The Renaissance room explodes: candlelight, swirling drapery, diagonals, drama. Baroque art is theatre that refuses to sit still — Caravaggio's spotlight, Rubens' motion.
look: Strong light-dark contrast (chiaroscuro)
Diagonals and billowing cloth create motion
Everything feels one second before climax

styles.name: Neoclassicism
styles.blurb: A stern correction to Baroque excess: clean outlines, marble surfaces, Roman virtue. Our variants include an oath-taking scene that turns cleanroom engineers into Roman citizens.
look: Sculptural figures with crisp contours
Marble, columns and restrained color
Poses quote Roman statues and reliefs

styles.name: Rococo
styles.blurb: The aristocracy at play: pastel silk, shell curves, garden swings and flirtation. Fragonard's swing hangs in this lesson's DNA — froth with world-class technique underneath.
look: Powdery pastels and golden light
Curves everywhere — no straight line survives
The mood is a garden party, slightly unreal

styles.name: Romanticism
styles.blurb: Feeling against reason: lone figures before fog, storms, ruins and the sublime — nature big enough to make humans tremble. Friedrich's wanderer and Turner's tempests lead the variants.
look: Vast weather dwarfs the figure
Light breaks through cloud like revelation
Ruins and cliffs stand for time and fate

styles.name: Pre-Raphaelite Painting
styles.blurb: Young rebels painted with jeweler's detail and jewel color: every leaf counted, literary heroines in real landscapes, intensity bordering on obsession.
look: Botanical, almost photographic detail
Saturated jewel colors in sharp focus
A melancholy, storybook stillness

styles.name: Tonalism
styles.blurb: Nearly one color: dusk, mist and hush. Tonalists traded detail for mood, painting the moment when the world goes quiet and forms melt into a single chord.
look: One dominant tone veils the whole scene
Details dissolve into mist
It feels like a memory, not a view

styles.name: Dutch Vanitas Still Life
styles.blurb: Beautiful objects with a warning label: wilting flowers, hourglasses, snuffed candles — worldly pleasures are brief. Our café table is restaged as a memento mori, the wafer as a golden disc among the props.
look: Deep darkness with a single raking light
Every object is a symbol of time passing
Rich textures: glass, petal, metal, crumb

styles.name: French Realism
styles.blurb: Paint what you see, at life size, without mythology: workers, stone-breakers, gleaners. Scandalous in 1850, it is now the ancestor of documentary everything. Our model joins fab workers at shift change.
look: Earthy, unglamorous palette
Labor is shown with dignity, not pity
No halos, no costumes — the present day

styles.name: Proto-Renaissance (Giotto)
styles.blurb: Around 1300, Giotto broke with flat medieval icons and gave painted people real weight, space and feelings. His figures stand on a shallow stage like actors, and their faces actually grieve, wonder and react. Our café scene becomes a solemn little drama, heavy with emotion.
look: Figures are solid and heavy, like statues wrapped in blue robes
The space is a shallow stage — just deep enough to stand in
Faces show real sorrow and tenderness instead of blank icon stares

styles.name: Early Netherlandish (van Eyck)
styles.blurb: Flemish painters like Jan van Eyck used oil paint to render the world at microscopic sharpness — every jewel, thread and reflection in place. Nothing is random: a candle, a mirror, a little dog all carry hidden meanings. She sits in a jewel-lit room where you could zoom in forever.
look: Impossibly fine detail — individual threads, beads and reflections
A convex mirror rounds up the whole room in one small circle
Light glows on jewels and polished surfaces like real oil paint

styles.name: Northern Renaissance
styles.blurb: North of the Alps, artists mixed Dürer's precise engraved line with Bruegel's teeming peasant panoramas and Bosch's strange imagination. Instead of one perfect hero, you get a whole busy world of proverbs, seasons and small human comedy. She shrinks to one figure in a crowded village scene.
look: She is small inside a huge, busy landscape full of tiny figures
Every corner hides a little scene — work, play, folly
Crisp engraved detail even in distant roofs and trees

styles.name: High Renaissance
styles.blurb: For a brief moment around 1500, Leonardo, Raphael and Michelangelo seemed to solve painting itself: perfect balance, calm beauty, bodies arranged in stable pyramids. Leonardo's sfumato — smoky soft edges with no hard lines — melts faces into gentle shadow. She becomes a serene, Madonna-like center of complete harmony.
look: The composition settles into a calm, stable pyramid
Edges are smoky and soft — sfumato, with no harsh outlines
Her expression is serene and idealized, beyond everyday emotion

styles.name: Venetian Colorism (Titian)
styles.blurb: Florence prized drawing; Venice prized color. Titian built flesh, silk and sunsets out of layered golden glazes, letting color itself do the modeling. The result is warm, lush and sensuous — paint that seems to glow from inside.
look: Golden, honeyed light washes over skin and fabric
Color is built in glowing layers rather than crisp outlines
A lush landscape concert setting, all richness and ease

styles.name: Mannerism
styles.blurb: After the High Renaissance achieved perfection, younger artists deliberately bent it: bodies stretched too long, poses twisted like serpents, colors turned acid and strange. Mannerism is elegance with an edge of unease. She elongates into a graceful, restless figure in a crowded vertical space.
look: Her body is stretched longer and more elegant than nature allows
The pose twists in a serpentine S-curve
Acid, off-key colors heighten the sense of unease

styles.name: Dutch Golden Age
styles.blurb: Seventeenth-century Holland produced two opposite geniuses of light: Rembrandt, who drowned scenes in golden shadow, and Vermeer, who filled quiet rooms with cool daylight from a window. This picture splits the difference — she pours her milk-coffee between darkness and daylight.
look: One side sinks into deep Rembrandt shadow and golden chiaroscuro
The other side glows with Vermeer's cool, even window light
An ordinary pouring gesture becomes the whole drama

styles.name: Spanish Golden Age (Velázquez)
styles.blurb: Velázquez painted the Spanish court with loose, seemingly effortless brushwork — and quietly made himself part of the scene. His masterpiece Las Meninas plays games with mirrors, glances and reflected royalty. Here she stands at the center of just such a room, where everyone seems to be looking at you.
look: Figures arrange themselves around her like a court portrait come alive
A mirror or reflection hints at royalty just out of view
Brushwork is loose and sketchy up close, exact from a distance

styles.name: French Classicism
styles.blurb: Poussin and Claude Lorrain believed painting should be rational: mythological figures arranged like a frieze, landscapes measured out in calm, golden order. Every tree and temple sits exactly where reason would put it. She joins a stoic procession in a landscape built like architecture.
look: Figures line up in a measured, frieze-like row
The landscape recedes in orderly golden planes
Gestures are stoic and deliberate — feeling kept under control

styles.name: Goya
styles.tag: From court painter to the Black Paintings
styles.blurb: Goya began as a cheerful court painter of bright tapestry designs and ended painting nightmares directly on his walls — Saturn, witches, firing squads. Reason and monsters wrestle through his whole career. This image splits his two worlds: festive color above, darkness below, and she stands between them.
look: Bright, tapestry-cartoon color fills the upper scene
Black-painting darkness and shadowy shapes press in below
Her figure is caught between the cheerful and the terrifying

styles.name: English Landscape (Constable)
styles.blurb: Constable painted his home county of Suffolk as if the sky were the main event — he made hundreds of cloud studies, chasing real weather. His oil sketches have a fresh, breezy energy that finished paintings often lost. Here towering clouds roll over a green valley mill scene, and she is small within it, sketchbook in hand.
look: Clouds take up most of the picture, built from sketchy, energetic paint
Fresh greens and damp English light fill the valley below
She is a small working figure inside the vast weather

styles.name: Hudson River School
styles.blurb: America's first great painters treated the wilderness as a cathedral: vast golden valleys, waterfalls and distant peaks rendered in glowing detail. Human beings appear tiny, humbled by the scale of nature. She stands small before a waterfall, awed like everyone who first saw these canvases.
look: A vast golden valley stretches to distant, glowing peaks
Her figure is tiny against the waterfall and wilderness
Every leaf and rock is lit with clear, luminous detail

styles.name: Barbizon School
styles.blurb: Before Impressionism, the Barbizon painters left the studio to paint the forest of Fontainebleau and the peasants who worked it, in quiet tonal browns and greens. Millet gave rural labor a still, monumental dignity. At dusk at the forest's edge, she gathers firewood in that same hushed mood.
look: Muted browns and greens melt into a tonal dusk
Peasants and cattle move slowly at the forest edge
Her firewood-gathering pose has Millet's quiet, monumental stillness

styles.name: Academic Art
styles.blurb: The official art of the 1800s prized flawless technique: porcelain skin, invisible brushstrokes, mythological subjects polished like marble. Bouguereau could paint a nymph so smoothly that critics accused him of using photographs. She appears as a water bearer in marble light, every surface perfected.
look: Skin and drapery are porcelain-smooth, with no visible brushwork
The pose borrows classical mythology — a nymph-like water bearer
Cool marble light idealizes everything it touches

styles.name: American Realism
styles.blurb: Thomas Eakins believed in honest looking — he studied anatomy and painted rowers, surgeons and boxers with scientific accuracy. Winslow Homer brought the same clear eye to sea light and outdoor life. Here she rows among athletes painted with anatomical honesty and bracing Atlantic light.
look: Muscles and rowing motion are rendered with anatomical precision
Hard, clear sea light — no romantic haze
The scene feels observed from life, like Eakins's rowing pictures

styles.name: Vedute (Canaletto)
styles.blurb: A veduta is a highly detailed city view, and Canaletto was its king: wealthy tourists bought his crystalline Venetian panoramas as souvenirs. Every cornice, gondola and ripple is exactly where it should be. She is a tiny figure on a bridge inside a perfect painted postcard.
look: Architecture is rendered with near-photographic exactness
Gondolas and figures dot the canal in crisp, even light
She is tiny on a bridge, one detail in the grand panorama

styles.name: Grand Manner Portraiture
styles.blurb: British Grand Manner portraits flattered sitters by dressing them in classical grandeur — silk gowns, columned terraces, noble landscapes. Reynolds elevated his subjects toward ancient heroes; Gainsborough softened them with feathery trees and shimmering fabric. She poses in silks, elevated and feathered at once.
look: She stands in elegant silks, posed like classical nobility
A grand landscape with classical touches opens behind her
Trees and foliage are painted with Gainsborough's feathery touch

styles.name: Chardin
styles.blurb: Chardin painted kitchen maids and copper pots with such tenderness that the humblest objects seem to glow with inner life. His soft grey-brown light and velvety paint turn chores into meditations. She becomes his kitchen maid, paused in a bubble of silence among the pots.
look: Soft grey-brown light wraps everything in hush
Copper pots and simple objects are painted with loving attention
Her paused, quiet pose feels like a held breath

styles.name: Orientalism
styles.blurb: Nineteenth-century European painters flooded Salons with scenes of the Middle East and North Africa — tiled palaces, harems, markets — often more fantasy than reportage. The best, like Gérôme, rendered tiles and textiles with jewel-like precision. She sits in such a gleaming tiled interior, a window into how Europe dreamed the East.
look: Tiles, arches and textiles are rendered in jewel-like detail
The architecture is an opulent, imagined palace interior
Her modern figure contrasts with the odalisque-era setting

styles.name: Nazarenes
styles.blurb: A brotherhood of young German artists in Rome, the Nazarenes rejected slick academic painting and tried to revive the sincere, crisp style of early Renaissance fresco. Their work is all clean outlines, bright local color and pious solemnity. She joins a fresco-like procession of earnest young artists.
look: Crisp, clean outlines define every figure and fold
Colors are bright and flat, like early Renaissance fresco
The procession of young figures is solemn and devout

styles.name: Luminism
styles.blurb: American Luminists painted water so still it became a mirror, with brushwork so invisible the surface looks like glass. Their calm, clear light feels almost supernatural — a held moment at dawn or dusk. She floats in a small boat on water that reflects the sky perfectly.
look: Water is mirror-still, doubling the sky exactly
No brushwork is visible — the surface is glassy smooth
Clear dawn light gives the scene a hushed, timeless calm

styles.name: Macchiaioli
styles.blurb: Macchiaioli means patch-makers: these Tuscan rebels built sunlight out of bold patches — macchie — of color laid side by side, sketching outdoors before the French Impressionists made it famous. Form dissolves into spots of light and shade. She stands in a sun-struck Tuscan field assembled entirely from patches.
look: Sunlight is built from bold, separate patches of color
Forms are simplified into spots of light and dark
Haystacks and leisure figures share the same patchy treatment

styles.name: Peredvizhniki
styles.blurb: The Peredvizhniki — the Wanderers — broke from Russia's academy and carried exhibitions of honest, socially aware painting to provincial towns. Repin painted barge haulers and processions with piercing psychological truth. Here she rests among the haulers on a great river, every face a story.
look: Faces are painted with deep psychological individuality
Laborers rest with real exhaustion, not heroic posing
Wide Russian river light spreads behind the group

styles.name: Naturalism
styles.blurb: Naturalist painters like Bastien-Lepage took Realism outdoors, painting peasants with almost photographic accuracy in bright, high-key daylight. No beautifying, no drama — just the honest field and the people working it. She gleans in a hayfield where every grass blade is told truthfully.
look: Bright, even outdoor light with no theatrical shadows
Every grass blade and worn fabric is honestly detailed
Her gleaning pose is unposed, caught from real labor

styles.name: Japonisme
styles.blurb: When Japan opened to trade in the 1850s, its woodblock prints electrified European artists: flat color, daring crops, diagonal bridges. Van Gogh even copied a Hiroshige plum-blossom scene in oils, adding his own border. Here she stands under plum blossom in a ukiyo-e composition translated into European paint.
look: Flat decorative color replaces Western shading and depth
A diagonal bridge cuts boldly across the composition
Plum blossom frames her in the manner of a Hiroshige print

lessons.title: Art in Public: Walls, Nations and Movements
lessons.bigIdea: Some art is made to persuade crowds, not decorate rooms — it gets big, legible and ideological.
lessons.intro: Mexican muralists painted national history on public walls; Harlem Renaissance artists forged a visual identity; Soviet Socialist Realism glorified the worker; the New Objectivity stared at Weimar Germany without blinking. Ask of every picture here: who paid for it, who was meant to see it, and what were they supposed to feel?
lessons.exercise: Pick the picture you would put on a public building to make people proud, and the one you would put in a newspaper to make them think. Defend both choices.

styles.name: Mexican Muralism
styles.blurb: After the Mexican Revolution, the state handed its walls to painters: history, labor and identity at architectural scale, readable by a crowd that might not read words. The variants channel Rivera's registers, Orozco's fire and Siqueiros' dynamism.
look: Figures are monumental, bigger than life
Stories unfold in stacked registers
Workers and machines are the heroes

styles.name: Harlem Renaissance
styles.blurb: Aaron Douglas's silhouettes and murals gave the Harlem Renaissance its graphic voice: flat forms, radiating light, African motifs and jazz-age rhythm, asserting identity and modernity at once.
look: Flattened, silhouette-like figures
Radiating arcs and rhythmic pattern
Gold, black and earth tones carry pride and energy

styles.name: American Regionalism
styles.blurb: Midwestern painters answered European modernism with rolling farmland, small towns and curved, rhythmic clarity — our fab rises from the prairie like a grain elevator.
look: Rolling, rhythmic landscape curves
Clean modeling with a storybook clarity
Local pride as subject matter

styles.name: Soviet Socialist Realism
styles.blurb: The mandated style of the Soviet state: academic realism put to heroic optimism — workers, engineers and collective triumphs, idealized and sunlit. Study it as both painting and persuasion. (Our version keeps the banners wordless.)
look: Heroic scale and confident poses
Bright, optimistic academic realism
Machinery and banners stage the message

styles.name: New Objectivity
styles.blurb: After Expressionism's fever, a cold eye: Dix and Schad painted cafés, portraits and streets with crystalline precision and quiet irony. Nothing is exaggerated, and that is what stings.
look: Razor-sharp, almost photographic detail
Cool, detached emotional temperature
Modern life observed without comfort

styles.name: Arts and Crafts
styles.tag: William Morris and the movement, from 1860s
styles.blurb: A rebellion against factory goods: honest materials, visible handwork, medieval-revival pattern. Morris's workshops wove, printed and built the café around our model — art you live inside.
look: Pattern drawn from plants, honestly stylized
Wood, textile and print textures everywhere
Nothing pretends to be another material

styles.name: Ashcan School
styles.blurb: In the 1900s a group of New York painters turned away from polite subjects and painted the city as it was — tenements, street crowds, boxers, workers on their breaks. The Ashcan School got its mocking nickname because critics thought trash cans were all they painted. Here the grit is real: she serves coffee to workers in a dark, charcoal-heavy street scene with the raw energy of a George Bellows boxing crowd.
look: Charcoal-dark paint and sooty tones dominate the whole scene
Workers crowd the street while she serves coffee among them
Brushwork feels hurried and physical, like the noise of the city itself

styles.name: Social Realism
styles.blurb: Social realism uses plain, legible pictures to tell the stories of ordinary people — migration, low wages, injustice — and to argue that those stories matter. Jacob Lawrence told the Great Migration of Black Americans northward in flat tempera panels, one episode at a time. Our panel borrows his language: she carries a suitcase and a wafer box northward, a worker in a much bigger journey.
look: Flat tempera shapes with almost no shading or perspective depth
She strides forward carrying a suitcase and a box of wafers
Earthy, limited colors arranged like panels in a story sequence

styles.name: New Deal Art
styles.blurb: During the Great Depression, the US government hired unemployed artists to paint murals in post offices and print posters for parks and public health. The style is optimistic and monumental: sturdy workers building dams, bridges and factories for a better tomorrow. In our mural she rivets alongside the crews building a dam and a fab — semiconductor plant — with the same heroic confidence.
look: Heroic, larger-than-life workers building a dam and a fab together
She rivets in line with the crew, an equal among giants
Smooth, sculptural figures and clear storytelling made for a public wall

styles.name: Wartime Propaganda Poster
styles.blurb: A propaganda poster is a picture with a job: recruit soldiers, sell war bonds, shame spies, keep factories humming. Designers used bold limited colors, one unforgettable figure and a pointing finger or slogan you could read from across the street. She takes the classic recruitment pose — pointing straight at you — with the riveter energy of Rosie and a grainy halftone print finish.
look: She points directly forward in the classic recruitment-poster pose
Only a few bold, flat colors carry the whole image
A grainy halftone dot texture mimics cheap wartime printing

styles.name: Graffiti and Street Art
styles.blurb: Graffiti began as a signature — a name written big and wild on subway cars and walls — and grew into street art: murals, stencils and paste-ups made for everyone who walks past, no ticket required. It is public art without permission, painted fast before anyone can stop you. Here her portrait is stenciled onto a brick wall beside wildstyle lettering, spray drips and all, at the scale of a city block.
look: Her portrait is stenciled flat onto a real brick wall surface
Wildstyle letters twist and interlock beside the portrait
Spray-paint drips and overspray soften the edges of the image

styles.name: Chicano Muralism
styles.blurb: In the 1960s and 70s, Mexican-American artists covered the walls of Southwest barrios with murals celebrating their heritage — Aztec calendars, revolutionary heroes, farmworkers, lowrider culture. The murals were history lessons, pride and protest in one, painted where the community actually lived. She appears as a community heroine on a neighborhood wall, airbrushed in lowrider colors beneath the Aztec calendar.
look: An Aztec calendar anchors the composition like a rising sun
Airbrush blends melt one vivid lowrider color into the next
She stands monumental as a heroine of the neighborhood, not a distant celebrity

styles.name: Feminist Art
styles.blurb: Feminist artists of the 1970s asked why art history remembered so few women, and answered by making work that honored women's lives and labor — including crafts like embroidery and ceramics that museums had dismissed as mere decoration. Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party set a monumental table with a place for each great woman of history. Our version sets a place for her, with embroidered and ceramic craft raised to monument scale.
look: A formal place setting honors her like a guest at a historic banquet
Embroidery and ceramic details are treated as monumental, not decorative
Craft textures — stitching, glaze, woven cloth — fill the image

styles.name: Black Arts Movement
styles.tag: AfriCOBRA and the Wall of Respect
styles.blurb: The Black Arts Movement of the 1960s and 70s insisted that Black art should serve Black communities — proud, political and joyful. Chicago's Wall of Respect mural honored Black heroes on a neighborhood building, and the AfriCOBRA collective made posters in what they called Kool-Aid colors: bright, shining and unapologetic. She joins a mural of heroes and family figures in that same radiant poster energy.
look: Kool-Aid colors — bright oranges, yellows and purples — glow across the wall
Proud family figures and heroes share the mural with her
Bold poster shapes stay readable from far down the street

styles.name: Chinese Revolutionary Poster
styles.blurb: During China's Cultural Revolution, posters showed model workers, peasants and soldiers beaming with health and certainty, bathed in the light of a red sun. The style — rosy cheeks, heroic poses, gouache-painted finish — was meant to teach everyone how to feel and whom to imitate. Our heroine holds a silicon wafer aloft like a model worker's tool, radiant rays streaming behind her.
look: She holds a wafer aloft in the heroic model-worker pose
Red sun rays radiate outward behind her figure
A smooth gouache poster finish gives skin a rosy, idealized glow

styles.name: Cuban OSPAAAL Posters
styles.blurb: From the 1960s, Havana's OSPAAAL organization shipped folded solidarity posters inside its magazine to liberation movements around the world. Printed in Day-Glo silkscreen inks, they fused fighters, flowers and flags into single unforgettable symbols. Here she appears in bold flat inks, merged with a guerrilla-flower image in that unmistakable fluorescent style.
look: Day-Glo fluorescent inks push the colors beyond natural saturation
Her figure fuses with a flower-and-fighter symbol image
Flat silkscreen shapes with no shading or modeling

styles.name: Polish Poster School
styles.blurb: After the Second World War, Poland's state film agency let artists design movie posters with almost total freedom — and they answered with surreal painted metaphors instead of stars' faces. One strange, poetic image had to carry the whole film. Our poster follows the rule: her coffee cup becomes a bomb of flowers, painted in loose gouache with barely any type at all.
look: A single surreal metaphor — a coffee cup exploding into flowers — carries the poster
Painterly gouache brushwork keeps the image loose and handmade
Almost no text: a wide minimal space is left where type would go

styles.name: May '68 Posters
styles.blurb: When Paris erupted in May 1968, art students occupied their school, renamed it the Atelier Populaire — the People's Workshop — and silkscreened hundreds of protest posters overnight. Each used one color, one bold image and a few words, printed rough and fast for the streets. She raises a wafer like a torch beside the factory-and-fist imagery, in that same urgent one-color print.
look: A single ink color does all the work, printed rough and fast
She raises a wafer overhead like a torch of protest
Factory chimneys and a raised fist share the bold silhouette style

styles.name: Taller de Gráfica Popular
styles.blurb: The Taller de Gráfica Popular, founded in Mexico City in 1937, was a workshop of printmakers who believed cheap prints could fight for workers, peasants and against fascism. Their weapon was the linocut broadside: stark black and white, bold carved shapes, sold for pennies or pasted on walls. In the spirit of Leopoldo Méndez, she leads a printmakers' strike scene in uncompromising black and white.
look: Stark black-and-white linocut shapes with no gray tones
She leads a crowd scene of workers and printmakers
Bold carved contours give every figure monumental weight

styles.name: Group of Seven
styles.blurb: In the 1920s, Canada's Group of Seven painted the northern wilderness — windswept jack pines, pink granite, cold lakes — as the true portrait of their young country. Their sketches, especially Tom Thomson's, are vigorous and weather-beaten, made outdoors in the wind. She is tiny in a red canoe on a Shield lake here: the land is the hero, and the human is just a note inside it.
look: A windswept jack pine twists against a dramatic northern sky
Pink granite rocks and a cold lake fill most of the canvas
She sits tiny in a small red canoe, dwarfed by the wilderness

styles.name: Heidelberg School
styles.blurb: Australia's Heidelberg School painters took French impressionism outdoors into the bush in the 1880s and 90s, and found a light Europe didn't have — blue distances and golden, heat-hazed air. Tom Roberts painted shearers and settlers as national heroes of work. She stands in that blue-and-gold landscape near a shearing shed, painted fast and fresh in open air.
look: Blue distant hills melt into golden, heat-hazed foreground light
A shearing-shed era landscape sets a pioneer working scene
Loose plein-air brushwork keeps the light shimmering and immediate

styles.name: Brazilian Modernism
styles.blurb: Brazil's modernists of the 1920s wanted an art that devoured European styles and digested them into something Brazilian — they called it Anthropophagy, cultural cannibalism. Tarsila do Amaral painted dreamlike landscapes of bulbous green hills and giant, playful figures. She wanders an Abaporu-like world here, monumental and strange among the swelling hills.
look: Bulbous, swelling green hills roll through a dream landscape
Her figure is giant and playful, with exaggerated proportions
Smooth, simplified shapes in saturated candy colors

styles.name: Indigenismo
styles.blurb: After the Mexican Revolution and across the Andes, indigenismo artists put Indigenous people at the center of national art — monumental figures in earth colors, carrying the dignity of labor and ancient heritage. It was identity-building with a political edge, kin to the Mexican muralists. She carries produce up terraced steps among towering figures, with Siqueiros-era gravity.
look: Monumental Indigenous figures tower in earth-colored paint
She carries produce up steep terraced steps
Heavy, sculptural bodies convey labor and dignity, not decoration

styles.name: Nigerian Modernism (Zaria)
styles.blurb: At the Zaria Art School in the late 1950s, young Nigerian artists rebelled against their colonial curriculum and proposed Natural Synthesis: fuse traditional Nigerian forms — like the curving uli lines of Igbo body painting — with modern oil painting. The result launched Nigerian modernism. Here uli line work flows through an oil-painted Lagos scene, and she stands where the two traditions merge.
look: Flowing uli curves wind through a modern oil-painted scene
A contemporary Lagos setting replaces any village stereotype
Traditional line and modern paint occupy the same figures at once

lessons.title: Modernism Breaks the Picture
lessons.bigIdea: Between 1870 and 1940 artists dismantled the window-illusion piece by piece: light, color, form, then reality itself.
lessons.intro: Impressionists painted light instead of things. Fauvists freed color from nature. Cubists showed several viewpoints at once. Surrealists and Dada artists attacked logic itself. Each style in this lesson breaks one rule the canon lessons taught you — see if you can name the rule being broken in each picture.
lessons.exercise: For each picture, complete the sentence: 'This artist cares more about ___ than about making it look real.' Compare your answers with a partner's.

styles.name: Impressionism
styles.blurb: Paint the light, not the thing: broken brushstrokes of pure color that fuse in the viewer's eye. The variants quote Renoir's terraces, Monet's riverbanks and Pissarro's boulevards — afternoons you can almost feel.
look: Visible, broken brushstrokes
Shadows are blue and violet, never black
The scene sparkles and breathes

styles.name: Pointillism
styles.blurb: Impressionism made systematic: thousands of distinct dots of pure color, mixed by your eye, not the palette. Stand close — confetti. Stand back — a sunny café.
look: The image is built only from dots
Colors vibrate where complements touch
Stillness and order beneath the shimmer

styles.name: Symbolism
styles.blurb: Against realism, a art of suggestion: jeweled palaces, crescent moons, peacocks and beautiful melancholy. Moreau, Klimt and Redon haunt the four variants — pictures that behave like dreams and poems.
look: Gold, jewel tones and moonlight
Ornament swallows the figure into pattern
Everything feels symbolic of something unnamed

styles.name: Fauvism
styles.blurb: Matisse and Derain let color off the leash: green skies, orange floors, pink light — chosen for feeling and harmony, not description. Critics called them fauves, wild beasts; they kept the name.
look: Colors are arbitrary and high-key
Forms simplify so color can lead
Even a cleanroom turns into a sunflower field

styles.name: Expressionism
styles.blurb: Distort the world to match the feeling: jagged streets, acid color, anxious crowds. Kirchner's tilted Berlin and Munch's unease drive these variants — the café as a state of mind.
look: Forms tilt, stretch and sharpen
Colors clash on purpose — acid green, blood red
Brushwork is agitated, never calm

styles.name: Cubism
styles.blurb: Break the object into facets and show several viewpoints at once. The café table, cup and sitter shatter into interlocking planes — then, in the synthetic variant, reassemble as bright flat shapes.
look: One object, several viewpoints, same canvas
Ochre and gray dominate the analytic variant
Glasses become twin circles; planes overlap like glass shards

styles.name: Futurism
styles.blurb: Speed as beauty: repeated limbs, motion echoes, city light streaking past. Boccioni and Balla painted what a photograph of movement feels like — our model multiplied across the boulevard.
look: The figure repeats in motion phases
Diagonal speed lines cut the scene
Machines and lights share the stage as equals

styles.name: Orphism
styles.blurb: Abstraction you can dance to: concentric discs and arcs of simultaneous color, named for Orpheus and music. Our model is woven into the swirl — present, but rhythm first.
look: Color arrives in discs and arcs
Complements vibrate against each other
The figure emerges from pure rhythm

styles.name: Surrealism
styles.blurb: Paint the unconscious: melting wafers in a desert, cups orbiting a dream room, a sea inside a teacup. Dalí's precision, Magritte's calm absurdity and Ernst's forests animate the variants — impossible things, rendered believably.
look: Impossible events painted with total conviction
Familiar objects misbehave quietly
Horizons and skies feel too clear, like dreams

styles.name: Dada Photomontage
styles.blurb: Hannah Höch and John Heartfield weaponized scissors and newspapers: photographs cut apart and recombined into absurd, satirical machines. Our model is quite literally assembled from clippings.
look: Visible scissor edges and halftone textures
Newspaper, gears and advertisements collide
Scale makes no sense, deliberately

styles.name: Cézanne
styles.blurb: Paul Cézanne rebuilt the world out of simple shapes — cylinders, spheres and patches of warm and cool color — and modern artists from Picasso onward called him their father. Here his beloved mountain, Mont Sainte-Victoire, rises behind her, and she sits like one of his card players, assembled from sturdy blocks of paint.
look: The mountain is built from flat, tilted patches of blue, green and ochre
Her figure is modeled in chunky warm-and-cool blocks rather than smooth shading
Everything — table, figure, landscape — is simplified toward cylinders and cubes

styles.name: Van Gogh
styles.blurb: Vincent van Gogh painted with thick, visible strokes and colors far more intense than real life, so a night sky swirls and a café glows like a furnace. Our café terrace sits under his churning stars, and every surface vibrates with directional brushwork.
look: The sky curls into spirals and waves of cobalt and white
Her figure is painted in short, separate strokes of citron yellow and blue
Dark cypress shapes rise like flames at the edge of the scene

styles.name: Gauguin and Synthetism
styles.blurb: Paul Gauguin and his friends decided a painting should be flat areas of pure color outlined in dark lines — like stained glass — chosen for feeling rather than accuracy. This Breton scene trades realistic shading for bold, symbolic color fields.
look: Large flat areas of pure color are fenced in by dark outlines
Colors are symbolic, not natural — the ground and fields glow in unreal reds and golds
Shading and perspective nearly disappear, so the scene reads like a tapestry

styles.name: Toulouse-Lautrec Posters
styles.blurb: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec turned Paris nightlife into posters: flat shapes, daring crops and a few acidic colors printed by lithography. Here she becomes a café-concert singer, spotlit in acid green against a crowd of black silhouettes.
look: The audience is reduced to a row of flat black silhouettes along the bottom
Her lit figure glows acid green and yellow against the dark
Shapes are simplified to poster-flat areas with almost no modeling

styles.name: Les Nabis
styles.blurb: The Nabis — a brotherhood of young French painters — made quiet domestic interiors where pattern matters more than depth. In Édouard Vuillard's manner, her dress dissolves into the wallpaper until figure and room become one decorative surface.
look: Her dress and the wallpaper share the same dense pattern, so she nearly vanishes into the room
The interior is flattened — tables, walls and figure sit in one shallow layer
Muted, tapestry-like colors cover every surface with small repeated motifs

styles.name: Vienna Secession
styles.blurb: Vienna's rebels mixed two extremes: Gustav Klimt wrapped his figures in real gold and ornament, while Egon Schiele drew bodies with raw, nervous line. She wears a Klimt-style golden robe of squares and spirals, drawn with a Schiele edge.
look: Her robe is a mosaic of gold squares, spirals and eye-like ornaments
Gold areas shine flatly instead of modeling round form
The visible face and hands stay simple and pale against the glittering pattern

styles.name: Der Blaue Reiter
styles.blurb: Der Blaue Reiter — 'The Blue Rider' — was a Munich group led by Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc, who believed colors carried spiritual meanings, blue above all. Her figure dissolves into prismatic mountains and Marc's famous blue horses, halfway to pure abstraction.
look: Blue horses gallop through the scene as symbols, not realistic animals
Mountains and sky break into prism-like wedges of saturated color
Her outline softens and partly melts into the surrounding color chords

styles.name: Naïve Art (Rousseau)
styles.blurb: Henri Rousseau was a self-taught Paris toll collector who painted dream jungles without ever leaving France. Borrowing his Sleeping Gypsy, she lies asleep in flat, lush foliage while a lion pads in to inspect her.
look: Every leaf and plant is painted flat, crisp and oversized, like cut paper
A lion stands calmly beside the sleeping figure in the moonlight
The scene feels still and dreamlike, with no realistic shadows

styles.name: Suprematism
styles.blurb: In 1915 Kazimir Malevich reduced painting to almost nothing: a black square on white, which he called the zero point of art. Our version keeps his floating geometry — a black square, a red rectangle standing in for her wafer — with her tiny figure adrift in the white infinity.
look: A plain black square floats near the top of an empty white field
A single red rectangle is the only warm, saturated shape
Her tiny figure hovers without ground, shadow or horizon

styles.name: Early Pure Abstraction
styles.blurb: Years before abstraction became famous, the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint was painting enormous diagrams of spiritual evolution — spirals, shells and symbolic flowers in soft pastel. She stands small inside one of these charts, as if her story were being mapped by symbols.
look: Huge pastel spirals sweep across the picture like diagrams
Symbolic flowers, shells and circles are arranged like a chart, not a scene
Her small figure is placed inside the diagram rather than dominating it

styles.name: Metaphysical Painting
styles.blurb: Giorgio de Chirico painted empty Italian piazzas at strange hours, where long shadows, arcades and statues create a dreamlike unease. She appears as a mannequin-like figure beside a classical statue, in light that feels like late afternoon and midnight at once.
look: Shadows stretch impossibly long across an almost empty square
Rows of dark arcades recede on two sides of the piazza
Her figure is stiff and mannequin-like next to a statue

styles.name: School of Paris
styles.blurb: The 'School of Paris' was not a school but the foreign artists — Chagall, Modigliani and others — who made Paris modernism cosmopolitan. This picture borrows Marc Chagall's floating lovers and village rooftops, with a Modigliani elegance in her long neck.
look: She floats weightlessly above rooftops, defying gravity like a dream
A goat and a bouquet of flowers drift beside her
Her neck and face are elongated in Modigliani's graceful manner

styles.name: Dada Readymade
styles.blurb: Marcel Duchamp scandalized art by declaring ordinary objects — a urinal, a bicycle wheel — to be sculptures simply because the artist chose them. Here her café cup gets the treatment: presented on a gallery plinth as a 'readymade', next to Duchamp's famous wheel.
look: Her everyday coffee cup sits on a museum plinth like a priceless sculpture
A bicycle wheel mounted on a stool stands beside it
The stark white gallery makes the ordinary objects look absurdly important

styles.name: Abstract Surrealism (Miró)
styles.blurb: Joan Miró built a private picture-language of stars, birds, ladders and wiggly creatures, scattered like constellations on deep blue. She joins the game as a whimsical glyph herself, reduced to a few playful signs.
look: Stars, ladders and bird-like signs float on a deep blue ground
Every form is a simple sign — dots, hooks and tadpole shapes
Her figure is simplified into one of the playful glyphs

styles.name: Kahlo and Mexican Modernism
styles.blurb: Frida Kahlo painted herself again and again, surrounded by the monkeys, plants and folk symbols of Mexico, turning pain and identity into direct, frontal portraits. She meets your gaze just as unflinchingly, framed by jungle growth and a folk-art ex-voto border.
look: Monkeys and lush plants crowd around her on both sides
Her gaze is frontal, steady and unsmiling, with a strong joined brow
A decorative folk border frames the scene like a small devotional painting

styles.name: Art Brut and Outsider Art
styles.blurb: Jean Dubuffet championed 'art brut' — raw work by self-taught outsiders and psychiatric patients, untouched by art school rules. In that spirit, her face repeats obsessively across a dense marker-and-crayon field that leaves no empty space, in the manner of Adolf Wölfli.
look: Her face repeats again and again across the whole surface
No space is left empty — pattern fills every gap (horror vacui)
The drawing looks like raw marker and crayon, deliberately unpolished

styles.name: Vorticism
styles.blurb: Vorticism was Britain's short, sharp answer to Futurism: art for the machine age, built from hard angles and crystalline shards. A London street shatters around her, and her figure becomes a faceted, engine-like form at the still center of the vortex.
look: The street breaks into sharp, crystalline shards and diagonals
Her figure is faceted like a machine or engine part
Colors are hard and industrial — grays, ochres and blacks

styles.name: Rayonism
styles.blurb: In Moscow around 1913, Natalia Goncharova and Mikhail Larionov proposed painting not objects but the rays of light bouncing off them. Her figure refracts into crossed beams of spectral color, dissolving into pure light and energy.
look: Diagonal beams of colored light cross the whole picture
Her figure breaks apart where the rays pass through it
Colors separate into spectrum bands like light through a prism

styles.name: Cubo-Futurism
styles.blurb: Russia's Cubo-Futurists smashed Cubist fragmentation together with Futurist speed, and printed wild artist books in an invented nonsense language called zaum. Her figure shatters into metallic cones and cylinders amid the chaos of a futurist book page.
look: Her body is rebuilt from metallic cones, cylinders and shards
Fragments overlap and collide as if the figure were exploding
The composition has the rough, hand-made chaos of an artist's book page

styles.name: Purism (Léger)
styles.blurb: Purism wanted modern painting to be as clean and ordered as a well-made machine, and Fernand Léger gave it tubular, robot-like figures. She becomes one of his bold outlined machine-women, standing among gears in flat primary colors.
look: Her limbs are smooth tubes and cylinders, like polished machine parts
Thick black outlines lock every shape in place
Gears and mechanical shapes share the flat red, blue and yellow palette

styles.name: Synchromism
styles.blurb: Synchromism — 'with color' — was America's first abstract movement, founded on the idea that color can be composed like music, in scales and chords. Rhythmic arcs of spectral color build her figure the way notes build a chord.
look: Sweeping arcs of rainbow color radiate through the composition
Colors are arranged in repeating scales, like musical runs
Her figure emerges from the color rhythms rather than from drawn outlines

styles.name: Magic Realism
styles.blurb: Magic realism paints the everyday world with perfect clarity — and then lets one impossible thing happen, very quietly. The café looks completely ordinary, except that her coffee cup floats in mid-air and a wafer glows on the table.
look: Everything is painted with sharp, hyper-clear, almost photographic detail
Her coffee cup floats impossibly beside her hand
A wafer on the table glows softly, the scene's one quiet miracle

styles.name: CoBrA
styles.blurb: CoBrA — named for Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam — was a postwar group that prized spontaneity, folk art and children's drawing over polish. Karel Appel's fierce, joyful manner turns her into a bright monster of raw paint.
look: Thick paint is smeared and splashed with visible, energetic gestures
Her figure is simplified like a child's drawing, with a fierce grin
Raw, unmixed colors clash at full strength

styles.name: Art Informel and Tachisme
styles.blurb: After the Second World War, many European painters abandoned form altogether for gesture and matter — tachisme means painting in stains and smears. Her silhouette barely surfaces from a storm of thick, dragged paint, as if the picture were still deciding whether to become a figure.
look: The surface is built from thick smears, drips and scraped stains of paint
Her silhouette only just emerges from the gestural storm
The palette is somber — earth, black and gray with flashes of color

styles.name: School of London
styles.blurb: While abstraction ruled, a London circle around Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud kept painting the human figure — with fleshy paint and psychological pressure. She sits on a bed-like platform inside one of Bacon's space-frame cages, exposed and intense.
look: Thin space-frame lines draw a cage-like box around her figure
Flesh is painted thickly, with heavy, worked surfaces like Freud's
The empty, dark background concentrates all attention on the isolated figure

lessons.title: Systems and Geometry: Art as Design
lessons.bigIdea: Twentieth-century artists and designers tried to build pictures from systems: grids, pure shapes, primary colors, optical laws.
lessons.intro: The Bauhaus, De Stijl and the Constructivists wanted a universal visual language. Op artists weaponized optical illusion; Abstract Expressionists did the opposite — huge, unsystematic gesture. Art Nouveau and Art Deco remind us that 'design' also means ornament, luxury and the curve. Notice how many of these styles still shape the apps and posters around you.
lessons.exercise: Find the picture with the fewest elements that still reads as 'TSMC at a café'. What is the minimum a picture needs?

styles.name: Art Nouveau
styles.blurb: The whiplash line: Mucha's posters turned hair, stems and smoke into one flowing system of ornament. The variants give our model the full treatment — halo, café terrace, allegory panel, theatre poster.
look: Sinuous, plant-like curves organize everything
A circular halo frames the figure like a jewel
Muted gold, sage and peach harmonize

styles.name: Art Deco
styles.blurb: Nouveau's curves grow up into geometry: sunbursts, chevrons, symmetry, gold on black. The style of skyscrapers, ocean liners and movie palaces — our model's natural habitat, honestly.
look: Strict symmetry and stepped forms
Gold, black and emerald luxury
Everything looks engineered and elegant

styles.name: Bauhaus Graphic Design
styles.blurb: A school that redesigned the world from first shapes: circle, triangle, square; red, yellow, blue. The variants build our model from pure geometry, Kandinsky's circles, Klee's play and Schmidt's typographic grids.
look: Primary shapes and colors do the drawing
Composition follows a visible grid or diagonal
Playfulness survives inside the system

styles.name: Constructivism
styles.blurb: Art as engineering for a new society: bold diagonals, red-black-cream photomontage, figures thrust forward like pistons. Text is banished in our variants — wafer discs carry the message instead.
look: Diagonals dominate; nothing sits level
Red, black and cream only
Photomontage scale shifts: giant profile, small figure

styles.name: De Stijl
styles.blurb: The strictest system of all: black lines, white ground, red-yellow-blue rectangles — and, hidden in our study, a seated figure. Proof that a person can survive total abstraction, barely.
look: Only horizontals, verticals and primaries
Balance is achieved without symmetry
The figure is a guest inside the grid

styles.name: Op Art
styles.blurb: Bridget Riley and Victor Vasarely turned retinal physics into art: stripes that bend, grids that swell, moiré that hums. Our model's profile appears as a shift in the pattern in one variant — find her in all four.
look: Patterns vibrate, warp or bulge
Black-and-white does most of the work
Your eyes feel the picture before your mind does

styles.name: Abstract Expressionism
styles.blurb: Painting as event: Pollock's dripped webs, de Kooning's fierce women, Rothko's glowing fields, Kline's black architecture. Our figure emerges from, dissolves into, and finally becomes four giant brushstrokes.
look: Gesture and scale replace description
The figure is found inside the paint, not under it
Each variant quotes a different giant of the movement

styles.name: Minimalism
styles.blurb: What remains when you remove almost everything? One figure, immense quiet, space doing the talking. Minimalism trusts the viewer to complete the work.
look: Vast emptiness is the main element
A single quiet figure anchors the void
Nothing decorative survives

styles.name: Swiss Style
styles.blurb: Grids, sans-serif type, asymmetry and objectivity: the design language that still runs every transit map and app. Our poster folds the café into red-black-white order, words replaced by pure shapes.
look: A strict grid organizes the layout
Red, black and white only
Asymmetry feels balanced and inevitable

styles.name: Precisionism
styles.blurb: Sheeler and Demuth painted factories like cathedrals: immaculate geometry, sharp light, no people, no dirt. Our fab machinery gets the same reverent, crystalline treatment.
look: Industrial forms simplified to pure geometry
Immaculate surfaces and hard light
Stillness — the machines seem to be holding their breath

styles.name: Color Field Painting
styles.blurb: In the 1950s, painters like Mark Rothko and Helen Frankenthaler let thinned paint soak straight into raw canvas, so color itself became the whole subject. There is almost nothing to 'look at' except a huge glowing expanse — and how it makes you feel standing in front of it.
look: One vast wine-red field fills nearly the whole picture
A single thin vertical stripe — Newman's 'zip' — cuts the field
She stands tiny at the edge, dwarfed by pure color

styles.name: Hard-Edge Painting
styles.blurb: Hard-edge painters of the 1950s and 60s, like Ellsworth Kelly and Frank Stella, rejected fuzzy brushwork completely. Every shape is flat, unmixed color with a razor-sharp border, arranged like pieces of a puzzle.
look: Flat color shapes meet at crisp, knife-clean edges
Concentric squares nest inside each other like a target
Her silhouette reads as one clean shape among the geometry

styles.name: Neo-Concrete Art
styles.blurb: Brazil's Neo-Concrete artists of the late 1950s thought stiff geometric art was too cold, so they made work you touch, wear and move. Lygia Clark built hinged metal sculptures to fold by hand, and Hélio Oiticica sewed capes — parangolés — that only become art when someone dances in them.
look: She wears a bright, flowing parangolé cape meant to be danced in
Hinged metal planes sit in her hands, ready to be folded
Color spills off the canvas and onto the body itself

styles.name: Plakatstil
styles.blurb: Around 1905, German poster artists stripped advertising down to one thing: a single bold product, huge and simplified, floating on an empty background. The style's name for it, Sachplakat, means 'object poster' — no scenery, no story, just the thing itself.
look: One object — her coffee cup — is enormous and dead simple
Flat, unshaded color with no texture or detail
The background is completely empty so nothing competes

styles.name: Streamline Moderne
styles.blurb: In the 1930s, designers borrowed the smooth curves of trains, ships and airplanes and put them on everything from toasters to diners. Long horizontal lines and rounded chrome corners made even a parked building look like it was speeding.
look: Horizontal speed lines streak along the walls and counter
Corners are rounded and wrapped in shiny chrome trim
She works as a waitress-engineer in a teal, aerodynamic café

styles.name: Mid-Century Modern
styles.blurb: After the Second World War, designers in America and Scandinavia filled homes with clean lines, warm wood and cheerful atomic-age patterns. It is the look of optimism: molded plywood chairs, starburst clocks and colors like mustard and teal.
look: Sculpted Eames-style chairs with spindly legs furnish the room
A sunburst clock and atomic boomerang patterns decorate the walls
Teak browns and mustard yellows warm the whole palette

styles.name: New Wave and Grunge Typography
styles.blurb: Starting with Wolfgang Weingart in the 1970s and exploding with David Carson's Ray Gun magazine in the 1990s, designers broke every rule of tidy type. Letters get torn, layered, stretched and half-buried — reading becomes an experience, not just information.
look: Layers of torn, overlapping type crash around her portrait
Photocopy grain and smudged noise rough up every surface
Words tilt, collide and break apart instead of lining up

styles.name: Flat Design vs Skeuomorphism
styles.blurb: Early phone apps used skeuomorphism — digital buttons dressed up as real leather, glass and stitched felt so they felt familiar. Around 2013, flat design threw all that decoration away for plain colored shapes. This picture splits the argument down the middle of her face.
look: The left half gleams with glass shine and stitched leather texture
The right half is plain flat vector shapes with no shadows
Her face crosses both halves, half realistic, half icon

styles.name: Isotype Pictograms
styles.blurb: In 1920s Vienna, Otto Neurath invented Isotype: a picture language for statistics, where one simple icon means a set number of things and more icons mean more of them. Charts could finally be read by anyone, in any language, at a glance.
look: Rows of identical little figures repeat like counting marks
She appears again and again as a simple worker pictogram
Only red and black ink carry the whole chart

styles.name: Wiener Werkstätte
styles.blurb: Founded in 1903, Vienna's Wiener Werkstätte workshops believed everything in life should be designed as one total artwork — furniture, fabric, jewelry, even cutlery. Josef Hoffmann's black-and-white grids and checkerboards became their unmistakable signature.
look: Black-and-white checkerboard geometry covers walls and surfaces
She wears a dress patterned with Hoffmann's strict grid
Silver workshop jewelry echoes the same squares and lines

styles.name: Japanese Postwar Graphic Design
styles.blurb: Japan's 1960s poster artists mixed pop color, photography and traditional woodblock imagery into joyful collisions. Tadanori Yokoo was the star: rising suns, Mount Fuji and ukiyo-e waves smashed together with psychedelic brightness.
look: Rising-sun rays fan out behind her portrait
Blue ukiyo-e waves curl through the pop-bright collage
Old Japanese motifs and 1960s colors crash into each other

styles.name: Classical Orders
styles.blurb: Ancient Greek and Roman builders worked from a kit of column styles — sturdy Doric, scroll-topped Ionic, leafy Corinthian — each with strict rules of proportion. For two thousand years, getting the orders right was what 'good architecture' meant.
look: Columns of different orders stand side by side for comparison
She poses as a caryatid — a statue-column — among them
Everything is calm, measured white marble symmetry

styles.name: Gothic Cathedral
styles.blurb: Medieval builders learned to push stone walls higher and thinner until they could be replaced by glass. Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and enormous rose windows turned cathedrals into cages of colored light reaching toward heaven.
look: Ribbed stone vaults soar far overhead like a stone skeleton
A glowing rose window pours colored light into the dark
She stands tiny, emphasizing how vertically huge the space is

styles.name: Islamic Architecture (Muqarnas)
styles.blurb: Muqarnas is a kind of three-dimensional geometry unique to Islamic architecture: hundreds of small carved cells stacked into a dome that looks like a stone honeycomb or a cave of stalactites. It dissolves the corner between wall and ceiling into pure pattern.
look: A honeycomb dome of stacked geometric cells hangs overhead
Turquoise and gold repeat in endless girih star patterns
She stands beneath the vault, small inside the geometry

styles.name: Baroque Architecture
styles.blurb: Seventeenth-century Baroque architects treated buildings like theater: curving walls, oval domes and shafts of light staged to overwhelm the senses. Bernini's Rome is the model — architecture as an emotional performance.
look: An oval dome swirls overhead instead of a plain round one
Dramatic shafts of light cut through the interior gloom
The colonnade curves around her like a stage set

styles.name: Beaux-Arts Architecture
styles.blurb: Trained at Paris's École des Beaux-Arts, this style planned grand buildings like classical symphonies: strict symmetry, sweeping staircases and every surface dressed with sculpture and gilding. It gave the world its opera houses, museums and railway stations.
look: A sweeping marble staircase fans out beneath her
Perfect symmetry organizes columns, statues and gilding
Classical orders pile up in layers of carved ornament

styles.name: International Style
styles.blurb: In the 1920s and 30s, architects like Le Corbusier and Mies van der Rohe stripped buildings to white boxes of glass and steel: no ornament, no history, just structure on stilts with long ribbon windows. It became the default look of offices and towers worldwide.
look: A glass curtain wall grids the tower into identical windows
The building floats on slim pilotis — thin support columns
Everything is white, flat and stripped of decoration

styles.name: Organic Architecture (Wright)
