styles.blurb: Frank Lloyd Wright believed a building should grow out of its landscape, not sit on top of it. His Fallingwater house of 1935 pours concrete terraces directly over a waterfall, mixing stone, glass and forest into one composition.
look: Flat terraces cantilever out over falling water
Rough horizontal stone bands echo the rock ledges
Trees and woods press in around the glass walls

styles.name: Postmodern Architecture
styles.blurb: By the 1980s, architects rebelled against the plain glass box by bringing back ornament, color and jokes. Postmodern buildings wear broken pediments, polka-dot columns and tops copied from antique furniture — serious structures with a wink.
look: A broken, split pediment crowns the building like a gag
Polka-dot columns turn structure into decoration
The rooftop copies a giant Chippendale furniture top

styles.name: High-Tech Architecture
styles.blurb: High-tech architects like Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano turned buildings inside out: ducts, pipes and escalators move to the outside, color-coded and on display. Paris's Pompidou Centre looks less like a museum than a cheerful machine.
look: Exposed ducts and tubes climb the outside of the building
Pipes are color-coded in bold primary colors
She rides an escalator tube attached to the exterior

styles.name: Metabolism
styles.blurb: Japan's Metabolist architects of the 1960s imagined cities as living organisms that grow by plugging in replaceable parts. Tokyo's Nakagin Capsule Tower bolted 140 tiny prefabricated room-capsules onto a concrete core, each one meant to be swapped out like a cell.
look: Small box capsules bolt onto a central concrete core
Her room is one plug-in pod among dozens of identical cells
The mood is 1970 Osaka expo-future: concrete, steel, optimism

styles.name: Parametric Architecture
styles.blurb: Parametric design lets computer algorithms generate a building's shape from flowing data, producing the seamless curves of architects like Zaha Hadid. Walls melt into floors, floors into ceilings, and the right angle nearly disappears.
look: White surfaces flow in one continuous wave with no seams
There is barely a right angle anywhere in the room
She walks through the curve as if inside a frozen liquid

lessons.title: Pop and After: Art in the Age of Mass Media
lessons.bigIdea: After 1960, art absorbed advertising, television, comics and consumer products — and started designing futures of its own.
lessons.intro: Pop Art held a mirror to supermarket culture. Psychedelic posters melted lettering into pure sensation. Memphis designers made furniture deliberately silly, Space Age designers sold tomorrow, and Afrofuturism claimed the future for Black imagination. The café scene keeps up with every one of these costumes.
lessons.exercise: Which picture here could be an advertisement, and what would it be selling? What makes the others resist being ads?

styles.name: Pop Art
styles.blurb: Soup cans, comics and advertisements, enlarged until they become icons. Lichtenstein's Ben-Day dots and Warhol's repeated portraits lead the variants — our model as comic heroine and as silkscreen grid.
look: Dots, flat ink and commercial color
Repetition turns a portrait into a brand
Speech balloons and product shots invade fine art

styles.name: Psychedelic Poster Art
styles.blurb: Fillmore concert posters melted Art Nouveau lettering into liquid, vibrating color — legibility sacrificed to sensation. Letterforms survive in our version as pure shapes inside the swirl.
look: Complementary colors vibrate at maximum volume
Shapes flow like liquid or smoke
The figure dissolves into the trip

styles.name: Memphis Design
styles.blurb: Ettore Sottsass's Memphis Group declared war on good taste: squiggles, terrazzo, pastel clashes, shapes that refuse to behave. Design as a joke that turned out to be liberation.
look: Squiggles, zigzags and terrazzo patterns
Pastel collides with black and primary brights
Nothing matches, on purpose, joyfully

styles.name: Space Age Design
styles.blurb: Starbursts, boomerangs and orbital rings: the future as imagined from a 1962 kitchen. Our café becomes a retro-future lounge, glossy white and orange under a ringed planet.
look: Atomic starbursts and boomerang shapes
Glossy white, orange and teal optimism
Everything looks like a toy rocket's interior

styles.name: Afrofuturism
styles.blurb: African heritage projected into cosmic technology: regal gold, adinkra-like motifs, starfields and advanced cities — a corrective to futures that left Black people out. Our model takes the throne under the stars.
look: Gold regality meets high technology
Starfields and cosmic scale
Traditional motifs redesigned as future insignia

styles.name: Neo-Dada
styles.blurb: In the 1950s, Robert Rauschenberg and Jasper Johns quietly rebelled against Abstract Expressionism's seriousness by bringing everyday stuff back into art — targets, flags, photos, junk. Neo-Dada is playful and deadpan at once: her portrait here is half painting, half collage of found things.
look: A painted target and flag motifs share the picture with her portrait
Faded photo-transfer textures ghost across the surface
Ordinary found objects are treated as seriously as brushstrokes

styles.name: Nouveau Réalisme
styles.blurb: France's answer to Pop Art: the New Realists used reality itself as material. Yves Klein covered things in his own patented blue and pressed painted bodies onto canvas, while Arman piled up hundreds of identical objects in boxes — here, her silhouette in blue beside a hoard of coffee cups.
look: One intense ultramarine blue swallows her silhouette whole
Her figure is a body-print — a shape stamped by a person, not drawn
A mass of repeated coffee cups is stacked up like sculpture

styles.name: Fluxus
styles.blurb: Fluxus artists in the 1960s treated art as a game anyone could play: a short written instruction — an 'event score' — was the artwork, and performing it could be as simple as pouring a drink. Here she performs a playful piece with a cup and a wafer, photographed like a humble event card.
look: The scene is staged like a black-and-white instruction card
Everyday props — a cup, a wafer — carry the whole performance
The mood is deadpan and funny rather than grand

styles.name: Conceptual Art
styles.tag: The idea is the work, LeWitt
styles.blurb: Conceptual artists of the late 1960s argued the idea behind a work matters more than the object itself. Sol LeWitt's wall drawings are just instructions that anyone can execute, and Joseph Kosuth famously displayed a chair, a photo of the chair, and its dictionary definition side by side — both appear in this gallery scene.
look: A huge wall of precise ruled lines rises behind her
A real chair, its photograph and a definition are arranged as one work
The room feels like an argument you walk through, not a picture you look at

styles.name: Arte Povera
styles.blurb: Arte Povera means 'poor art' — Italian artists in the late 1960s rejected polished gallery art and built works from rags, twigs, soil and scrap. The humble materials become monumental here, with one flash of neon and even a sculpture railed with living lettuce.
look: Rags, branches and rough scraps are given museum importance
A tube of neon cuts through the earthy materials
A living plant is part of the sculpture, so the work keeps changing

styles.name: Capitalist Realism
styles.blurb: In 1960s West Germany, Gerhard Richter and Sigmar Polke mocked both socialist realism and consumer advertising with 'Capitalist Realism'. Richter blurred photographs into paintings; Polke printed with benday dots and strange chemical stains. Her portrait splits down the middle between the two tricks.
look: One half of her face is smeared into a soft photographic blur
The other half is built from coarse printed dots
Odd brownish stains bloom like alchemy experiments

styles.name: Neo-Expressionism
styles.blurb: In the late 1970s and 80s, painting roared back — big, fast and emotional. Jean-Michel Basquiat crowned his figures and scrawled anatomy and crossed-out words around them, while Anselm Kiefer dragged history into thick paint. This portrait has that raw, urgent energy.
look: A scribbled crown hovers over her head
Anatomical sketches and scratched-out words crowd the background
Color is laid on in raw, aggressive oil-stick strokes

styles.name: Pictures Generation
styles.blurb: Around 1980, artists like Barbara Kruger and Cindy Sherman started stealing images from advertising and film to expose how media manipulates us — a strategy called appropriation. Kruger's signature is a black-and-white photo slashed with bold white-on-red text bars, imitated here with the lettering left abstract.
look: A grainy black-and-white photograph does the talking
Bold red bars with white lettering cut across the image
The whole thing reads like an ad arguing with itself

styles.name: Young British Artists
styles.blurb: The Young British Artists exploded out of London in the 1990s with shock tactics and slick presentation: Damien Hirst preserved animals in glass tanks and covered walls with grids of colored spots. Here she gets the vitrine treatment — preserved like a specimen beside a spot wall.
look: She is displayed inside a glass case like a museum specimen
A neat grid of colored spots covers the wall beside her
Everything is polished and clinical, which makes it stranger

styles.name: Superflat
styles.blurb: Takashi Murakami named his style Superflat: Japanese art squashed into glossy, depthless surfaces, mixing cute cartoon characters with traditional flat painting. Smiling flowers and jellyfish eyes swirl around her anime figure here — adorable and slightly overwhelming at once.
look: Grinning cartoon flowers bloom in every gap
Jellyfish with staring eyes drift around her
There is almost no shadow or depth — everything is surface

styles.name: Lowbrow and Pop Surrealism
styles.blurb: Lowbrow grew out of hot-rod culture, underground comics and punk flyers before sneaking into galleries. Its pop-surrealist wing loves big-eyed girls, tiki bars and custom cars, all painted with a glossy, obsessive finish — her portrait here joins a tiki and a hot rod.
look: Hot-rod green glows against deep shadow
Her eyes are enlarged in classic big-eye girl style
A tiki figure and a customized car share her spotlight

styles.name: Contemporary Figuration
styles.blurb: Figurative painting — pictures of people — is thriving again, led by artists like David Hockney and Kehinde Wiley. Wiley poses everyday people like Renaissance royalty against patterns so dense the background swallows the sitter. She is enthroned the same way here, in heroic pose against a floral flood.
look: Flowers and vines crawl over the whole background and onto her space
Her pose is borrowed from old royal portraits — chin up, fully frontal
Pattern and person compete for who is in front

styles.name: Chicago Imagists
styles.blurb: In 1960s Chicago, the Hairy Who group made art that was funny, grotesque and packed to bursting — inspired by comics, circus posters and shop-window signs. Gladys Nilsson filled every inch with wiry little figures. Her portrait here is swallowed by the same cheerful pattern madness.
look: Wiry cartoon figures squirm into every corner
No empty space survives — the surface is dense with detail
The drawing is deliberately awkward, rubbery and comic

styles.name: Pattern and Decoration
styles.blurb: In the 1970s, Pattern and Decoration artists rebelled against minimalism's bare grids by covering everything in ornament — Islamic tiles, floral fabrics, decorative traditions the art world had dismissed as 'craft'. Layer upon layer buries her figure here until person and pattern become one shimmering field.
look: Islamic-style geometry and floral motifs overlap in layers
Her outline nearly dissolves into the decoration
More is more — there is no resting place for the eye

styles.name: Neo-Geo
styles.blurb: Neo-Geometric Conceptualism — Neo-Geo for short — was the cool, cynical geometry of the 1980s. Peter Halley painted day-glo 'cells' connected by conduits, diagrams of a society run like a circuit board. She is drawn into that diagram here, a figure wired into the system.
look: Fluorescent rectangles glow like cells on a circuit board
Thick conduit lines connect every shape, including her
The geometry is crisp and airless — a simulation, not a place

styles.name: Sots Art
styles.blurb: Sots Art was the Soviet Union's underground answer to Pop Art: Komar and Melamid mixed heroic socialist-realist posters with Western consumer brands to expose both propagandas at once. Here a Soviet poster heroine raises a Coke in one hand and a wafer in the other — two ideologies in one heroic pose.
look: Her pose copies the striding heroes of Soviet posters
A Coke bottle gets the same heroic treatment as the wafer
Two visual languages — poster red and advertising gloss — are double-exposed

styles.name: Chinese Political Pop
styles.blurb: In 1990s China, artists like Wang Guangyi collided Cultural Revolution propaganda with Western brand imagery — his 'Great Criticism' posters stamp logos over revolutionary heroes. Her portrait uses the same layout: propaganda figures massed behind her, fenced in by flat bars of brand color.
look: Rows of propaganda-style figures stand behind her like a poster crowd
Flat bars of pure brand color slice across the composition
Her calm portrait sits at the collision point of two systems

styles.name: Post-Internet Art
styles.blurb: Post-Internet art is made by artists who grew up online: instead of posting images to the web, they drag web aesthetics back into the gallery — stock photos, screens and glossy 3D renders become physical objects. Her image multiplies across tilted screens and pools of shiny resin here.
look: Screens lean at careless angles, all showing versions of her
Glossy resin pools spread across the gallery floor
The lighting has the flat brightness of a stock photograph

styles.name: Vaporwave
styles.blurb: Vaporwave began as an internet music-and-image style that remixed 1980s consumer culture into a dreamy, ironic nostalgia. Its collage recipe never changes: a classical Roman bust, palm trees, a checkerboard floor and a pastel grid sunset. She gets the full treatment here.
look: A marble Roman bust wears her features
Palm trees and a black-and-white checkerboard floor frame the scene
Chrome shapes and a pastel sunset grid glow behind her

styles.name: Glitch Art
styles.blurb: Glitch artists make beauty from digital failure — corrupted files, compression errors and misbehaving software. Techniques like datamoshing smear pixels across the frame, and her portrait here is dissolving into exactly that kind of beautiful breakage.
look: Her image streaks sideways in smeared bands of pixels
Red, green and blue copies of her edges split apart
Blocky compression artifacts chew at the smooth areas

styles.name: Cyberpunk
styles.blurb: Cyberpunk is the rain-slick future of 1980s science fiction: megacities, neon signs, body tech and the slogan 'high tech, low life'. She stands in a steaming neon alley here, techwear on and a wafer glowing in her hand like contraband.
look: Neon signs reflect off wet pavement and steam
Her wafer glows like a piece of high technology
The alley is crowded, dark and lit only by advertising

styles.name: Synthwave
styles.blurb: Synthwave is nostalgia for a 1980s future that never happened — the look of arcade games and VHS covers, revived by the OutRun aesthetic. A chrome sun sinking over a glowing grid and purple mountains: she poses in front of it like the heroine of a 1984 that exists only in posters.
look: A striped chrome sun sets over a glowing perspective grid
Mountains and sky are pure purple and magenta
Her jacket and pose quote 1980s action-poster heroes

styles.name: Steampunk
styles.blurb: Steampunk imagines the future as the Victorians might have built it — steam engines, brass, gears and airships instead of computers. She appears here as an airship engineer, goggles up and a mechanical wafer in hand, surrounded by pipes and clockwork.
look: Brass goggles and exposed gears cover the machinery
Steam pipes coil through the background
Her wafer is rebuilt as a clockwork device

styles.name: Solarpunk
styles.blurb: Solarpunk is science fiction with hope: futures where technology and nature grow together, full of gardens, solar glass and art-nouveau curves. Against the leafy terraces of a green city, she tends a rooftop garden café — the future as a garden party.
look: Plants spill over every terrace and railing
Solar glass and greenery share the same surfaces
The curves borrow from art nouveau, not from machines

styles.name: Y2K Aesthetic
styles.blurb: The Y2K aesthetic is the turn-of-the-millennium future as pop culture imagined it around 1999: liquid chrome blobs, frosted translucent plastic, iridescent bubbles and chunky pixel fonts. She strikes a pop-star pose inside that shiny time capsule here.
look: Liquid chrome blobs float around her like mercury
Frosted, see-through plastic textures catch rainbow light
Pixel-style lettering shapes frame her pose

lessons.title: Beyond the Frame: Space, Light and Performance
lessons.bigIdea: Eventually artists left the rectangle entirely: art became landscape, architecture, light, movement and action.
lessons.intro: Land artists rearranged deserts. Light and Space artists made perception itself the artwork. Gutai painters attacked canvas with their bodies; kinetic sculptors set art spinning; stage designers and stop-motion animators built worlds that exist only in time. Our model still poses — but the 'picture' now surrounds her.
lessons.exercise: For each work, answer: if you stood inside it, where would you be and what would move? Which work would change most if you visited on a windy day?

styles.name: Land Art
styles.blurb: Robert Smithson spiraled a jetty into the Great Salt Lake; our version spirals stones and wafers across a desert flat, with the artist tiny inside her own drawing. The landscape is the canvas, and weather is a collaborator.
look: The artwork is visible fully only from the air
Materials come from the site itself
The human figure is a speck in the work

styles.name: Light and Space
styles.blurb: Turrell and Irwin made light itself the material: rooms of haze and color where edges vanish and your own perception becomes the exhibit. Our model softens into wine-red and amber atmosphere.
look: Color has no visible source or edge
The figure dissolves into atmosphere
Seeing itself is the subject

styles.name: Brutalist Architecture
styles.blurb: Béton brut — raw concrete — raised into monumental, shadow-carved masses. Our fab complex looms like a fortress, and the café table shrinks to a human footnote.
look: Board-formed concrete texture everywhere
Huge masses, deep shadow reveals
The person is small; the building is the portrait

styles.name: Deconstructivist Architecture
styles.blurb: Gehry and Hadid broke the box: titanium shards, tilted walls, colliding geometries that look mid-explosion, frozen. Our model sits calmly inside the beautiful wreckage.
look: Forms tilt, fracture and collide
No wall agrees with another
Calm figure, chaotic space

styles.name: Kinetic Sculpture
styles.blurb: Calder's mobiles turned sculpture into slow weather: balanced discs and rods rotating on air currents. Ours hangs wafer discs above our model, who has become part of the mechanism.
look: Balance and rotation are the composition
Shadows move as the piece moves
Engineering and poetry are the same act

styles.name: Gutai
styles.blurb: 'Concreteness': Gutai artists wrestled paint itself — flinging, pouring, breaking through paper — letting material act. Our model is mid-performance, wine-red paint in flight across raw canvas.
look: Paint is thrown, not brushed
Raw canvas and splashes are the image
The body of the artist is a tool

styles.name: Ballets Russes Stage Design
styles.blurb: Diaghilev's company fused painting, music and dance into total theatre, and Bakst's sets — exotic, ornate, drenched in color — redesigned European taste. Our model takes the principal's bow.
look: The whole stage is one ornamental painting
Costume and set share the same patterns
Color is theatrical: emerald, gold, flame

styles.name: Stop-Motion
styles.blurb: A handmade world photographed one frame at a time: clay, felt and miniature furniture, with the maker's fingerprints left in. Our café set is a tiny stage, charm included.
look: Visible clay and felt textures
Miniature furniture, slightly imperfect
It looks photographed, because the set 'exists'

styles.name: Installation Art (Kusama)
styles.blurb: Installation art turns a whole room into the artwork, and Yayoi Kusama is its polka-dot queen. Her mirrored Infinity Rooms multiply lights and reflections forever — here she stands inside one, surrounded by glowing dotted pumpkins, feeling both wonder and a little dread.
look: Her reflection repeats endlessly in the mirrored walls
Polka dots cover the pumpkins, the floor and the figure alike
Tiny points of light stretch away like a galaxy

styles.name: Performance and Happenings
styles.blurb: In performance art the artist's own body and actions are the artwork — nothing remains afterward but photographs and stories. The free-form Happenings of the 1960s blurred art into everyday life, and this grainy scene catches her mid-action, performing a scored gesture with a cup before a puzzled audience.
look: The grainy black-and-white look of old documentary photographs
A 1960s audience watches an ordinary action treated as art
The cup becomes a prop in a deliberate, scored gesture

styles.name: Video Art (Paik)
styles.blurb: Nam June Paik, the father of video art, treated television sets as sculptural material — stacking them into robots, walls and gardens. In his TV Garden, monitors sprout among living plants; here she sits among the glowing stacks, her face playing on every screen at once.
look: CRT television sets are stacked like building blocks
Plants grow between and around the glowing screens
Her face repeats on screen after screen, slightly different each time

styles.name: Assemblage
styles.blurb: Assemblage is sculpture built from found objects — scraps, bottles, maps and toys arranged until they start to dream. Joseph Cornell packed his poetic worlds into wooden shadow boxes, and this one shrinks her whole café into a box: bottles, maps, little birds and a silicon wafer for a moon.
look: Everything fits inside one shallow wooden box frame
Unrelated objects — bottles, maps, birds — share one small world
A wafer disc hangs in the box like a moon

styles.name: Site-Specific Wrapping (Christo)
styles.blurb: Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped entire buildings, bridges and coastlines in fabric, turning familiar landmarks into mysterious soft sculptures for a few weeks at a time. Here a whole chip fab is shrouded and roped, and she stands tiny before it — the drawing studies beside the scene are part of how the real projects were funded and planned.
look: The building's shape is still readable under its fabric skin
Ropes and seams pull the cloth tight like a parcel
She is drawn tiny, so the wrapped giant feels monumental

styles.name: Process Art
styles.blurb: Process artists cared less about the finished object than about what materials do on their own — sagging, melting, scattering, rusting. Eva Hesse hung latex and rope; Richard Serra splashed and propped lead. This studio scene lets gravity be the co-author, with sheets slumping and a wafer form hanging to test its pull.
look: Materials slump, droop and scatter instead of holding neat shapes
A wafer form hangs so gravity visibly acts on it
The studio floor is part of the artwork, not just beneath it

styles.name: Mono-ha
styles.blurb: Mono-ha, the School of Things, arose in Japan and Korea around 1968. Its artists placed raw materials — a stone, a glass plate, a beam — in careful relation and then stepped back, letting the arrangement itself be the art. This nearly empty room is the point: one stone, one plate, one still figure, and the space between them humming.
look: Almost nothing is in the room — emptiness does the talking
Natural stone and industrial glass sit in deliberate balance
Her stillness matches the objects; nobody is performing

styles.name: Immersive Projection (teamLab)
styles.blurb: The Japanese collective teamLab fills dark rooms with projected waterfalls, flowers and schools of fish that respond when visitors touch them. The picture is never finished and never the same twice. Here the digital garden blooms straight across her dress, and the walls react to her hand.
look: Projected flowers bloom over her dress as well as the walls
Light seems to move like water through the whole room
Her touch is part of the picture — the image answers back

styles.name: Modern Sculpture
styles.blurb: Modern sculptors reinvented the human figure three ways: Rodin left bronze rough and emotional, Brâncuși polished forms down to smooth eggs and birds, and Henry Moore hollowed reclining bodies into landscape-like abstractions. This garden triptych shows all three versions of her side by side — same model, three centuries of sculptural thinking in one lawn.
look: The Rodin figure's bronze surface is rough and hand-worked
The Brâncuși version is polished to a seamless egg-like shine
The Moore figure reclines with holes pierced through the body

styles.name: Classic Hand-Drawn Animation
styles.blurb: Golden-age cartoons were drawn by hand, one frame at a time, inked onto clear cels and laid over painted backgrounds. The result glows with 1930s Technicolor warmth. Her café pose here is a single frame from that world — you can almost see the slight shimmer where the cel meets the backdrop.
look: A crisp ink outline separates her from the painted background
Background colors are soft and watercolor-like, figures are flat and bright
The palette has the warm saturation of 1930s Technicolor

styles.name: Rubber-Hose Animation
styles.blurb: The earliest cartoon stars — think of the first Mickey Mouse shorts — had limbs like rubber hoses: no joints, no bones, just bendy tubes that bounced to the music. Everything in this black-and-white world wiggles, including her dance with a cup, and the pie-cut eyes are pure 1930s.
look: Her arms and legs bend in smooth curves with no elbows or knees
White gloves and pie-cut eyes mark the 1930s cartoon look
The whole scene is black and white and mid-bounce

styles.name: UPA Limited Animation
styles.blurb: The UPA studio rebelled against Disney's realism with limited animation: flat shapes, bold modernist design and movement suggested rather than fully drawn, as in Gerald McBoing-Boing. She is rebuilt here from a handful of simple shapes and textured color fields — proof that style can replace detail.
look: Her figure is built from a few flat, simple shapes
Backgrounds are textured fields of color, not realistic places
Movement feels snappy and stylized rather than lifelike

styles.name: Silhouette Animation (Reiniger)
styles.blurb: Lotte Reiniger made the oldest surviving animated feature in 1926 from jointed paper cut-outs, filmed as black silhouettes against glowing colored backgrounds. It is shadow puppetry with a camera. Her profile here is pure black paper — identity carried entirely by the outline.
look: Figures are solid black with no interior detail at all
Tiny joints at shoulders and elbows let the cut-outs move
The background glows in layers of colored glass tones

styles.name: Rotoscope
styles.blurb: Rotoscoping means filming real actors, then tracing over the footage frame by frame, so drawn characters move with uncanny lifelike smoothness. Ralph Bakshi used it for epic fantasy in the 1970s. Her café pose here keeps that painted-over-reality shimmer — realistic motion wearing an illustrated skin.
look: Movement lines look fluid and photographic underneath the drawing
Colors sit slightly loose over the forms, like paint on film
The realism feels dreamlike rather than crisp

styles.name: German Expressionist Cinema
styles.blurb: German films of the 1920s like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari built crooked sets and painted shadows directly onto the walls, so the world itself looked anxious and mad. Nothing here stands straight: the street tilts, the shadows are jagged ink, and she plays the heroine wandering through a nightmare fairground.
look: Walls and streets lean at impossible, tilted angles
Shadows are painted on as solid jagged shapes
Sharp contrasts of black and white make everything feel haunted

styles.name: Film Noir
styles.blurb: Film noir — the shadowy crime cinema of 1940s Hollywood — lit its scenes through slats and smoke so faces were sliced by stripes of light. This frame gives her the full treatment: venetian-blind shadows, a wet street shining behind her, and a haze hanging in the air.
look: Stripes of light and shadow from venetian blinds cross her face
Wet pavement mirrors the street lights below
Most of the frame stays dark; only edges and highlights glow

styles.name: Noh Theatre
styles.blurb: Noh is Japan's centuries-old theatre of stillness: masked actors move with glacial slowness across a bare stage painted with a single pine tree, while a chorus chants. The main actor, the shite, wears a carved wooden mask whose expression seems to shift with the light. She holds that frozen, fan-in-hand stillness here.
look: A carved mask replaces her face, expression fixed yet shifting
Brocade robes carry the color; the stage stays almost empty
The painted pine on the back wall is the only scenery

styles.name: Kabuki
styles.blurb: Kabuki is Noh's flamboyant opposite: all spectacle, bold kumadori makeup streaked in red and indigo, swirling costumes, and dramatic mie poses frozen at emotional peaks while the audience applauds. Actors charge down the hanamichi runway through the crowd. She strikes her mie mid-runway, gesture held like a thunderclap.
look: Kumadori makeup streaks the face in bold red lines
The pose is frozen mid-gesture, larger than life
A runway juts through where the audience would sit

styles.name: Chinese Opera
styles.blurb: In Peking opera, a painted face is a readable code — red for loyalty, white for treachery, gold for gods — and long white water sleeves extend every gesture into flowing calligraphy. She appears here in an embroidered robe mid-gesture, sleeves streaming, the whole story told by color and movement rather than scenery.
look: Painted-face colors signal character at a glance
Extra-long white sleeves trail from her hands like ribbons
The embroidered robe carries more scenery than the bare stage

lessons.title: Comics and Illustration: Pictures That Tell Stories
lessons.bigIdea: Some pictures are made to be read, not just looked at — in panels, on covers, in books, and on skin.
lessons.intro: Illustration is art with a job: sell the story, explain the plant, sell the dress, sell the magazine. This lesson runs from four-color comic panels and Hergé's clear line to botanical plates, fashion croquis, pulp covers and tattoo flash. The drawing styles differ wildly, but every one is engineered to communicate at a glance.
lessons.exercise: Pick two pictures that show the same café moment. Which one could you 'read' fastest from across the room, and what did the artist sacrifice to get that speed?

styles.name: American Comic Book
styles.blurb: Golden-age American comics were printed cheaply in four ink colors on newsprint, with shading built from fields of Ben-Day dots. The limits became the look: bold black ink, flat heroic color, everything framed in a panel border. She strikes her heroic café pose inside that border, dots and all.
look: Tiny Ben-Day dots build the shading and skin tones
Thick black ink outlines keep every shape punchy
A panel border frames the scene like a single comic frame

styles.name: Ligne Claire
styles.blurb: Ligne claire — clear line — is the drawing style Hergé perfected in Tintin: every object outlined in the same even black line, filled with flat color, no shadows or hatching anywhere. The world becomes calm, readable and quietly funny. Her café scene follows the rules exactly, down to the little dog-like robot at her side.
look: Every outline is the same clean, even weight
Colors are perfectly flat with no shading or gradients
Backgrounds are detailed but never distract from the figures

styles.name: Caricature and Editorial Cartoon
styles.blurb: Caricature stretches a face's most telling features until the likeness becomes an argument. Honoré Daumier aimed that weapon at judges and kings in 1830s lithographs; editorial cartoonists still fire it daily. Here her features get the Daumier treatment while a courtroom of nodding chip-fab executives dozes behind her.
look: Her key features are exaggerated but still unmistakably her
The scratchy lithograph line gives everything a printed bite
Background figures are drawn as a sleepy, nodding chorus

styles.name: Golden Age Illustration
styles.blurb: In the decades around 1900, deluxe storybooks paired lush printed plates with the text — Arthur Rackham's gnarled, whispering trees, N. C. Wyeth's bold frontier drama. A gilt-edged plate like this one was the picture a child fell into before reading a word. She stands as the storybook heroine, framed like a treasure.
look: A decorative gilt-edged frame marks it as a book plate
Trees twist into gnarled, characterful shapes behind her
Rich, muted colors feel printed on cream paper

styles.name: Children's Picture Book
styles.blurb: A picture book tells its story mostly through images, with a few warm words per page and shapes simple enough for a small child to read at a glance. This spread keeps the gouache shapes soft and the composition uncluttered — she reads aloud to a circle of small robot children under a tree, with calm space left where the text would go.
look: Shapes are simple, soft and easy to read instantly
Gentle gouache textures keep every color warm
Empty, calm space is left open for the story's words

styles.name: Botanical and Scientific Illustration
styles.blurb: Scientific illustration exists to teach: every leaf vein, seed and cross-section drawn with exact, measured precision so a reader can identify the real thing. This plate gives the treatment to a coffee plant and a silicon wafer alike — dissected, arranged and labeled — with her portrait watching from an oval roundel, like the author frontispiece of an old treatise.
look: Plants and wafer are shown whole and cut open side by side
Fine, exact linework records every vein and edge
Her portrait sits in an oval frame like an author's frontispiece

styles.name: Fashion Illustration
styles.blurb: Before fashion photography took over, illustrators sold elegance with ink: Erté's art-deco goddesses, and today's quick croquis — the elongated, nine-heads-tall sketch figure every designer starts from. Her cleanroom tunic is reimagined here as a runway gown, drawn in flowing ink with touches of gold.
look: Her figure is stretched to elongated, runway proportions
Loose ink lines suggest the garment more than describe it
Gold accents pick out details against the minimal sketch

styles.name: Underground Comix
styles.blurb: In the late 1960s, underground comix like R. Crumb's Zap burst out of San Francisco head shops — self-published, uncensored and drawn in dense, sweating cross-hatch. Everything bulges, leers and wobbles with street energy. Her panel keeps the café pose but drowns it in that gloriously unruly ink.
look: Dense cross-hatching builds every shadow by hand
Forms bulge and sweat with exaggerated street energy
The panel feels photocopied, raw and proudly unpolished

styles.name: Pulp Cover Art
styles.blurb: Pulp magazines were cheap fiction sold by their covers: lurid, brilliantly painted scenes of peril and wonder, with wide space at the top for the magazine's name. A cover had about two seconds to grab a browser at the newsstand. She gets the full treatment — space heroine, ray gun in hand, a ringed wafer planet burning behind her.
look: Bold empty space at the top waits for a masthead
Her pose is mid-drama, ray gun raised against the sky
Painted colors are lurid and saturated, built to shout

styles.name: Technical and Architectural Drawing
styles.blurb: Technical drawing is pictures as information: exact elevations, dimension lines and standard symbols that a builder or machinist can trust to the millimeter. Rendered as a blueprint — white line on deep blue — her café pose becomes an engineering elevation, measured and annotated like a machine part.
look: White lines on deep blueprint blue reverse the usual drawing
Dimension lines and arrows measure the figure and furniture
The pose is shown as a flat elevation, front-on and exact

styles.name: Tattoo Flash (American Traditional)
styles.blurb: Tattoo flash is the design sheet pinned up in a tattoo shop: ready-made images in American traditional style — bold black outlines, a tight palette of red, green and ochre, zero fussy shading — pioneered by sailors' artist Sailor Jerry. Her portrait becomes one bold flash design, eagle-and-banner style, ready to ink.
look: Outlines are thick, black and completely confident
The palette sticks to a few flat, punchy colors
The design sits on a plain sheet like a shop flash page

styles.name: Irezumi
styles.blurb: Irezumi is Japan's traditional full-body tattoo art: dragons, koi, waves and peonies flow together across the skin in one continuous composition, often built around open skin left as breathing space. This design wraps those motifs around her figure the way a bodysuit tattoo would, every wave and scale placed to follow the body's curves.
look: Dragons, waves and peonies flow together without gaps
Motifs bend and follow the curves of the body
Deep traditional colors sit against areas of bare skin

styles.name: Concept Art
styles.blurb: Concept art is the working drawing of the entertainment industry: before a film or game is built, artists explore characters in pages of painted thumbnails, variations and annotated callouts. This sheet treats her as a production design problem — same character, many quick painted possibilities, notes pointing at the details that matter.
look: Several thumbnail versions of her explore different ideas
Callout lines point to costume and prop details
Painting is fast and sketchy — thinking, not finishing

lessons.title: The Pixel Ladder: Video Game Graphics
lessons.bigIdea: Game graphics are art styles dictated by hardware. Every era's look is a negotiation between imagination and memory chips.
lessons.intro: Climb the ladder one console at a time. The NES could show only a handful of colors per sprite; the SNES multiplied them; the PlayStation split into lush 2D and wobbly low-polygon 3D; each generation since added polygons, light and physics. Because the pose never changes, you can watch pure rendering evolve — the same lesson as Lesson 1, played on machines.
lessons.exercise: Cover the labels and arrange the pictures oldest to newest by look alone. Then check: which single visual cue (pixels? polygons? reflections?) was most reliable?

styles.name: Pixel Art
styles.blurb: Every pixel placed on purpose. Born from hardware limits, kept as a discipline: limited palettes, readable silhouettes, dithering for gradients. Compare the sunset variant's dithered sky with the watercolor in Lesson 1 — same problem, opposite tools.
look: A strict grid underlies every curve
Dithering fakes extra colors
Silhouette stays readable at tiny size

styles.name: NES 8-Bit
styles.blurb: The NES palette held 54 colors, and each sprite could use only a few — so artists became economists. Our café runs on chunky pixels, flat color and hard outlines: charm extracted from scarcity. (Rendered a little finer than real hardware sprites, honestly.)
look: Huge, visible pixels
Flat colors with black outlines
Backgrounds simplify into tiles and shapes

styles.name: SNES 16-Bit
styles.blurb: Thousands of colors on screen, finer pixels, real shading: the 16-bit generation could finally do atmosphere. The same café gains dusk, glow and detail the NES could only imply.
look: Finer pixels, smoother curves
Dithered gradients and richer palettes
Backgrounds become places, not tiles

styles.name: PS1 2D Sprites
styles.blurb: While 3D grabbed headlines, 2D quietly peaked: high-resolution hand-drawn sprites over painted, pre-rendered backgrounds in games like Legend of Mana. Our café is lush, crisp and faintly soft with CRT warmth.
look: Hand-drawn sprite over a painted world
Background detail exceeds the character's
A slight softness, like a good CRT

styles.name: PS1 3D Low-Poly (FF7 Era)
styles.blurb: First-generation 3D: a few hundred polygons per character, flat Gouraud shading, textures that swim and warp. Final Fantasy VII's field screens paired these blocky figures with gorgeous pre-rendered backgrounds — the contrast is the era's signature.
look: Angular, faceted models with chunky hands
The background is far prettier than the model
Textures wobble if you imagine it moving

styles.name: PS1 3D Refined (DOA Era)
styles.blurb: By the original Dead or Alive, PS1 models had multiplied their polygons: rounded joints, texture-mapped faces, cleaner shading — still low-res and wobbly at heart, but unmistakably smoother. The ladder's middle rung.
look: Rounded, smoother silhouettes than the FF7 rung
Faces are textures, not geometry
Low-res softness lingers over everything

styles.name: PS3 / PS4 HD 3D
styles.blurb: HD real-time rendering: high-polygon models, normal maps faking fine detail, soft shadows and cinematic depth of field. The café is now a cutscene — polished CGI that still, visibly, comes from a game engine.
look: Soft shadows and shallow focus
Fabric and skin have surface detail
Clean, cinematic, but not yet photographic

styles.name: PS5 Ray-Traced
styles.blurb: Ray tracing simulates light itself: true reflections in the window and cup, soft global illumination, skin that scatters light. The ladder tops out near photography — compare with Lesson 3's photorealism and ask what, if anything, still gives the game away.
look: Reflections behave physically correctly
Individual hair strands and skin pores
Light bounces the way it does in rooms

styles.name: Stylized 3D Rendering
styles.blurb: Not every modern game chases realism: stylized rendering keeps 3D's freedom but paints its surfaces — soft studio light, smooth materials, a game-cinematic look that ages gracefully because it never pretended to be a photo.
look: Smooth, toy-like material perfection
Lighting is soft and designed, not simulated
It reads as '3D illustration', proudly

styles.name: Vector Arcade
styles.blurb: Before screens could fill in shapes, games like Asteroids (1979) drew everything with glowing lines on a vector monitor — the same technology as an oscilloscope. The café becomes a wireframe of pure light on black.
look: Everything is drawn in thin glowing green lines only
No filled shapes anywhere — the world is pure outline
Black background makes the geometry float like a radar screen

styles.name: Game Boy Monochrome
styles.blurb: Nintendo's Game Boy of 1989 had a tiny screen with exactly four shades of pea-soup green and chunky pixels. Artists turned that poverty into a charm all its own, and the café shrinks into a pocket-sized RPG room.
look: Only four shades of green exist in the entire picture
Chunky square pixels make every edge stair-stepped
The café reads as a tiny handheld adventure-game room

styles.name: Isometric Pixel
styles.blurb: Isometric games tilt the world at a fixed diamond angle, so rooms look like floating dollhouse dioramas you can peer into. Pixel artists loved it: every tile, chair and tiny prop placed by hand, one dot at a time.
look: The café floats as a cutaway room on a diamond-shaped base
Floor tiles form a neat diagonal diamond grid
Tiny hand-placed props — cups, chairs, plants — dot the room

styles.name: Pre-Rendered CG Sprites
styles.blurb: In 1994, Donkey Kong Country stunned players with characters that looked like glossy 3D models — but the home console couldn't do 3D, so the models were rendered on powerful SGI workstations and flattened into sprites in advance. The trick gave 16-bit games a plastic, airbrushed sheen.
look: She has a glossy, plastic-rendered sheen like a toy model
Painted backgrounds sit slightly apart from the shiny characters
Highlights look airbrushed, smooth and a little artificial

styles.name: N64 3D
styles.blurb: The Nintendo 64 of 1996 brought real 3D home, but with tiny memory: models are built from few polygons and textures smear into a famous blur. Add distance fog to hide the draw distance, and you get the era's unmistakable look.
look: Faces and furniture are chunky low-polygon shapes
Textures look smeared and blurry, like a photo through Vaseline
Fog fades the background so the world can end early

styles.name: PS2 / Dreamcast / GameCube Era
styles.blurb: Around 2000, the '128-bit' consoles — PlayStation 2, Dreamcast, GameCube — made 3D models smooth and clean at last, with shiny reflective surfaces and the first modern lighting tricks. Cutscenes started to look like cartoons you could almost watch as films.
look: Models are smooth and rounded, no longer chunky
Shiny specular highlights gleam on hard surfaces
The framing feels like a polished 2001 game cutscene

styles.name: Cel-Shaded 3D
styles.blurb: Cel shading makes real 3D models pretend to be hand-drawn cartoons: flat colors, simple shadows and bold outlines, as in Jet Set Radio and The Wind Waker. The café becomes a cartoon you can walk around in.
look: Flat toon colors replace realistic shading
Bold dark outlines trace her figure and the furniture
Shadows fall in one or two simple flat steps

styles.name: Voxel
styles.blurb: A voxel is a pixel with volume — a tiny cube. Build a world from millions of them, as Minecraft did, and everything from mountains to coffee cups becomes blocky sculpture.
look: Every object, including her, is assembled from small cubes
Stair-stepped blocky edges replace all curves
The café looks like a miniature diorama built from toy blocks

styles.name: ASCII and 1-Bit
styles.blurb: The earliest computer art had no pictures at all — only letters, numbers and symbols. Roguelike games and ASCII artists build whole worlds from keyboard characters, where an @ can be the hero and shading is just denser typing.
look: Her portrait is built entirely from text characters
Dense symbols make the darks; sparse ones make the lights
Only black and white exist — one bit, no gray

styles.name: Modern Low-Poly Indie
styles.blurb: Today's independent game artists choose low polygons on purpose: big flat-shaded facets, soft pastel colors and gentle fog. What was once a hardware limit is now a fashion — minimal, calm and stylish.
look: Large flat facets shade every surface in a single tone
The palette is soft pastel with drifting fog
Detail is stripped away until only elegant shapes remain

styles.name: Hand-Painted Textures
styles.blurb: Some 3D games wrap their models in textures painted by hand, brushstroke by brushstroke, instead of photographs or flat color. The world ends up looking like a storybook illustration you can walk through.
look: Visible brushstrokes cover walls, floor and furniture
Colors blend like paint rather than plastic or photo
She fits the same painterly treatment as her surroundings

styles.name: HD-2D
styles.blurb: Square Enix's HD-2D style, famous from Octopath Traveler, mixes old and new: charming pixel-art sprite characters wander through 3D miniature sets lit like dioramas. Tilt-shift blur and glowing bloom make the tiny world feel precious.
look: She is a pixel-art sprite standing in a 3D miniature café
Tilt-shift blur softens the top and bottom edges of the scene
Warm bloom makes lights and windows glow like a diorama
